154	# Concentration of Training Workloads Is the Cornerstone Principle of Block Periodization
155	
156	**What it is** — Issurin states the Block Periodization Concept (BPC) rests on one
157	foundational principle, concentration of training workloads, from which two others follow:
158	(1) a minimal number of targeted abilities per block, because highly concentrated loads
159	"only provide sufficient training stimuli to improve the targeted ability," and (2)
160	consecutive (not simultaneous) development of abilities, because "the number of decisive
161	abilities exceeds the number of abilities that can be developed simultaneously" (PDF p. 37,
162	printed p. 26, Figure 1.7). The rationale is laid out as a table of contradictions in the
163	traditional, simultaneous-development model for high-level athletes (Table 1.4, PDF p. 20,
164	printed p. 9): concurrent workloads compete for limited energy supply, differing
165	physiological-system restoration times leave athletes under-recovered for all targets at
166	once, workloads interact negatively (energy deficits, technical complexity, neuromuscular
167	fatigue), mental concentration cannot be split across many targets, and the training
168	stimulus needed for a high-level athlete's progress cannot be reached when it is divided
169	among many abilities.
170	
171	**Why it works** — Issurin's own explanation is that above a threshold of athletic level,
172	a quality only responds to a training stimulus concentrated enough to exceed that
173	threshold; splitting the same total training time across many qualities keeps each one's
174	stimulus below that threshold. He does not give a quantitative mechanism for where that
175	threshold sits or how "concentrated enough" is defined for a given ability or athlete — the
176	principle is argued from coaches' and scientists' collective experience (Table 1.4) rather
177	than derived from a stated dose-response model.
178	
179	**When to apply** — Designing training blocks for advanced, high-level athletes juggling
180	more qualities than can be trained well at once (the explicit target population, per
181	Issurin). **Eric's baseline:** this converges with the department's own compatibility rule,
182	"you can't ride two horses with one saddle" — incompatible qualities are not both trained at
183	full intensity in the same block (`method-baseline.md`, "Periodization and programming,"
184	citing `01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md` pp.28-29). It also converges with
185	[[periodization--bompa/principle--concentrated-loading-overreaching]], which independently
186	describes concentrated, saturated loading on one quality with a delayed 4-12 week rebound.
187	
188	**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — Issurin's own text (PDF p. 44, printed p. 33) states the
189	traditional, complex (simultaneous multi-ability) model "has visible benefits for the
190	preparation of low- and mid-level athletes": it is "more diversified, attractive and
191	lively," and medium-level concentration is "sufficient stimulation" at that level — the
192	concentration principle is explicitly scoped to high-performance athletes, not a universal
193	programming rule. **Contested:** Issurin's blanket claim elsewhere in the same chapter that
194	the traditional model "does not work well for high-performance athletes" (PDF p. 19,
195	printed p. 8) is disputed by this library's own Bompa & Haff 5th-edition material
196	(`periodization--bompa`), which is a current (not 1984-vintage) textbook still teaching and
197	defending a form of the traditional/complex periodization model for high-level athletes.
198	Issurin's critique in this chapter names Bompa's *1984* edition specifically (PDF p. 13,
199	printed p. 2) as one of the texts that propagated the traditional model he is arguing
200	against — it is not a critique of the Bompa & Haff 5th edition already in this library,
201	which incorporates concentrated-loading and conjugated-sequence ideas closer to Issurin's
202	own. **Inference:** Issurin's own later peer-reviewed review (2016, *Sports Medicine*,
203	"Benefits and Limitations of Block Periodized Training Approaches," Zotero item
204	`PT9QTQ2I`, not yet full-text-cached in this ingest) is titled around limitations as well as
205	benefits and likely narrows this 2008 book's confident framing; treat the frontmatter
206	`confidence: contested` as applying specifically to the universal "traditional doesn't work
207	for high performers" claim, not to the narrower, self-limited concentration principle.
208	
209	**Example** — A collegiate football strength staff trying to develop max strength,
210	aerobic capacity, alactic power, and technical skill acquisition all at full intensity in
211	the same 4-week block, per Table 1.4's logic, risks under-stimulating all four rather than
212	meaningfully improving any one; concentrating the block on 1-2 of them (with the rest held
213	at a retention dose) is the alternative Issurin argues for.
214	
215	**Related** — [[framework--block-periodization-mesocycle-taxonomy]] — the three-block
216	structure this principle produces. [[periodization--bompa/principle--concentrated-loading-overreaching]]
217	and [[periodization--bompa/framework--step-loading-paradigm]] — converging concentrated-load
218	ideas already in this library. [[supertraining--verkhoshansky/principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]] (staging) —
219	check for overlap on why generalized simultaneous training under-delivers for advanced
220	athletes.

235	# No More Than Three Training Modalities Per Workout, With 65-70% of Time on One or Two
236	
237	**What it is** — Issurin extends the concentration principle to single-session design
238	(Figure 2.4, PDF p. 75, printed p. 63; Table 2.12, PDF p. 76, printed p. 65) with five
239	stated rules (PDF p. 75, printed p. 64): (1) a workout should contain **no more than three
240	training modalities** — typically one dominant, one compatible with the main purpose, and
241	one for technique/tactics improvement or restoration; (2) **65-70% of total training time**
242	in a development workout should go to one or two selected modalities, to preserve workload
243	concentration; (3) after a key-workout, the following session should show a significant
244	load reduction — running two consecutive key-workouts is possible but risks excessive load
245	concentration; (4) hypertrophy-focused sessions require workload to be "substantially
246	reduced" for **at least 20 hours** afterward to protect the anabolic phase of muscle
247	restoration; (5) limiting modality count matters most in high-performance training —
248	junior/developmental athletes' programs can be more diverse and multilateral. Figure 2.4
249	maps which modalities are compatible as secondary/tertiary additions to five dominant ones:
250	aerobic endurance pairs with alactic sprint, strength-endurance-aerobic, and
251	hypertrophy-strength (placed after); anaerobic glycolytic endurance pairs with
252	strength-endurance-anaerobic, aerobic restoration, and mixed aerobic-anaerobic endurance;
253	alactic sprint pairs with aerobic endurance, explosive strength, hypertrophy-strength
254	(after), and aerobic restoration; hypertrophy-strength pairs with neural-strength, flexibility,
255	and aerobic restoration; new-technical-skill learning pairs with any modality, but only
256	*after* the dominant task. Table 2.12 gives the physiological/psychological rationale for
257	several of the strongest pairings (e.g., aerobic endurance + strength endurance: increased
258	oxidation supports the resistance work; alactic sprint + aerobic endurance: brief sprints
259	break monotony and keep a wide muscle-fiber pool activated for the subsequent aerobic work).
260	
261	**Why it works — the specific numeric thresholds are asserted, not derived** — The
262	underlying logic is the same concentration principle from Chapter 1
263	([[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]]): splitting a session across too many
264	modalities dilutes the stimulus for all of them. **Inference:** Issurin gives no stated
265	derivation for why the cutoff is exactly three modalities rather than two or four, why the
266	time-share threshold is 65-70% rather than some other range, or why 20 hours is the specific
267	reduced-load window after hypertrophy work (versus, e.g., 24 or 48 hours) — these read as
268	the author's own practical rules of thumb built from coaching experience rather than
269	citations to a dose-response study.
270	
271	**When to apply** — Auditing whether a practice plan or lift is trying to do too much:
272	count distinct training modalities in a session and check whether one or two of them
273	actually receive the majority of training time, per the 65-70% rule. Use Figure 2.4/Table
274	2.12 to check whether a planned secondary modality is a known-compatible pairing or an
275	unaddressed combination. **Eric's baseline** independently states a directionally identical
276	rule for compatibility, though at the block level rather than the single-session level:
277	"incompatible qualities... are not both targeted at full intensity in the same block"
278	(`method-baseline.md`, "Periodization and programming," citing
279	`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md` pp.28-29, "you can't ride two horses with one
280	saddle") — this Issurin entry gives that same instinct a specific numeric structure (≤3
281	modalities, 65-70% time-share) that the baseline material does not currently specify at
282	either the block or session level.
283	
284	**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — Treat the ≤3-modality, 65-70%, and 20-hour figures as
285	Issurin's own heuristics rather than established constants — no citation or underlying data
286	is given for any of the three in this chapter. Issurin explicitly narrows the number
287	constraints to high-performance training; junior/developmental programming is stated to
288	reasonably need more variety, not fewer modalities. Figure 2.4's compatibility map is not
289	exhaustive (it covers five dominant modalities, not every possible combination) — an
290	untested pairing should not be assumed incompatible or compatible by default; Issurin gives
291	no guidance for modalities not shown in the figure.
292	
293	**Example** — A practice plan combining strength-endurance, aerobic-anaerobic conditioning,
294	maximal-speed sprint work, and new-install technical work in one session would have four
295	distinct modalities, exceeding the stated ≤3 rule; per Figure 2.4, glycolytic endurance
296	pairs well with strength-endurance-anaerobic and aerobic restoration, but maximal speed and
297	new technical skill acquisition would need to be reduced to secondary/tertiary roles or
298	moved to a separate session to keep the session within the concentration guideline.
299	
300	**Related** — [[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]],
301	[[heuristic--exercise-sequencing-by-fatigue-state]],
302	[[framework--key-workout-and-key-exercise-concept]].

316	
317	# Accumulation, Transmutation (Transformation), and Realization: the Three Mesocycle-Blocks
318	
319	**What it is** — Issurin's core structural unit is the mesocycle-block, one of three types
320	(Table 1.7, PDF p. 37, printed p. 26): **Accumulation** targets basic abilities (aerobic
321	endurance, muscular strength, basic coordination) with high volume/reduced intensity and
322	"reasonable restoration"; **Transmutation** targets sport-specific abilities (special
323	endurance, strength endurance, proper technique) with reduced volume/increased intensity,
324	and explicitly does *not* provide full restoration — fatigue accumulates; **Realization**
325	targets integrative, competition-ready preparedness (model performances, maximum speed,
326	event-specific tactics) at low-medium volume/high intensity, with full restoration required
327	going in. Each type has its own monitoring focus: basic-ability tests for accumulation,
328	sport-specific-ability tests for transmutation, and maximum speed/strategy checks for
329	realization. **Locator note:** the 1985 origin paper (Issurin & Kaverin) and this book's
330	1.2.1 narrative (PDF p. 33, printed p. 22) use the term **transformation**; from section
331	1.2.2 onward (PDF p. 37+, printed p. 26+) and in the book's own tables, the term used is
332	**transmutation**. Both names refer to the same middle block; record both because a search
333	for either term should resolve to this entry.
334	
335	**Why it works** — The sequencing is designed to exploit the fact that different motor
336	abilities have different **residual training effect** durations (see
337	[[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]]): basic abilities (aerobic
338	endurance, max strength) decay slowest, so they can be built early and coast on their own
339	residual while transmutation and realization narrow the focus toward faster-decaying,
340	more specific and speed-dependent qualities close to competition. Issurin frames this as
341	superimposition of residual effects (Figure 1.8, PDF p. 39, printed p. 28) rather than
342	concurrent development of everything at once.
343	
344	**When to apply** — Structuring a training stage (the accumulation-transmutation-realization
345	sequence, ending in competition) for advanced athletes who need multiple qualities peaked
346	together — see [[framework--training-stage-and-multi-peak-annual-cycle]] for how these three
347	blocks compose into a full annual plan. **Eric's baseline** shows a structurally similar but
348	independently-arrived-at sequence: the department's own preparatory-period design goes
349	hypertrophy/work-capacity, then basic strength, then strength-to-power
350	(`method-baseline.md`, "Periodization and programming," citing week1-lecture.md pp.43-48) —
351	a general-to-specific progression that parallels accumulation-to-realization, though the
352	baseline's sequence is not explicitly framed with Issurin's residual-effect superimposition
353	logic or his restoration-status distinctions between blocks.
354	
355	**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — This is a three-way classification built for advanced
356	athletes who can tolerate the fatigue-accumulating transmutation block (see
357	[[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]] for the low-/mid-level-athlete
358	carve-out). It presumes a training stage that ends in a real competition or test date to
359	absorb the realization block's tapering logic; without a fixed target date, there is no
360	clear trigger for when accumulation should end and transmutation begin. **Contested (partly):**
361	the vault's Bompa & Haff material (`periodization--bompa/principle--concentrated-loading-overreaching`)
362	independently describes a comparable saturated-load-then-restitution structure with a
363	4-12 week delayed rebound — a longer and less rigidly three-staged model than Issurin's
364	roughly two-month training stage (below); the two should be read as convergent but not
365	identical prescriptions, and a program note should say which model's timing a given plan
366	follows.
367	
368	**Example** — A training stage built for a mid-season peak: 3-4 weeks of accumulation
369	(aerobic base, general strength), 3-4 weeks of transmutation (sport-specific conditioning,
370	strength-endurance, technique under fatigue), then 1-2 weeks of realization (tapered
371	volume, high-intensity model-speed work, full restoration) ending at the target competition
372	or test date.
373	
374	**Related** — [[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]],
375	[[framework--training-stage-and-multi-peak-annual-cycle]],
376	[[case-study--bondarchuk-hammer-throw-block-mesocycles]] (a different three-block taxonomy
377	from the same era, worth distinguishing from this one),
378	[[periodization--bompa/principle--concentrated-loading-overreaching]],
379	[[periodization--bompa/framework--step-loading-paradigm]].
380	######## framework--training-stage-and-multi-peak-annual-cycle.md
381	---
382	type: library-entry
383	kind: framework
384	domain: strength-and-conditioning
385	book: block-periodization--issurin

387	topic: training stage structure and multi-peak annual planning
388	category: [periodization, peaking, annual-plan, programming]
389	confidence: supported
390	ingest-tier: full-text
391	created: 2026-09-26
392	---
393	
394	# The Training Stage (A-T-R + Competition) Is the Annual Plan's Building Block, Enabling Multiple Peaks
395	
396	**What it is** — Issurin's annual cycle is built from a sequence of **training stages**,
397	each one containing all three mesocycle-blocks (accumulation, transmutation, realization) in
398	order, ending in a competition (PDF p. 38, printed p. 27). Each training stage "gives the
399	appearance of an annual cycle in miniature" — a block resembling a preparatory period
400	(accumulation), one resembling a competition period (transmutation), and a tapering block
401	ending in competitive performance (realization) (PDF p. 39, printed p. 28). The duration of
402	a training stage is set by how long the constituent residual training effects can be
403	superimposed (Figure 1.8; see
404	[[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]]) and "should be about two
405	months," though Issurin notes stages can run shorter near season's end or longer earlier in
406	the season, in which case "special measures should be used to prolong residual training
407	effects" (unspecified in this chapter — likely developed in Chapter 3, not yet ingested).
408	The number of training stages in a season "usually varies from four to seven," depending on
409	the sport's competition calendar (PDF p. 40, printed p. 29, Figure 1.9). Issurin lists five
410	claimed benefits of this design over the traditional model (PDF p. 40, printed p. 29, and
411	Table 1.8, PDF p. 42, printed p. 31): reduced total training volume without reducing workout
412	count; more purposeful monitoring (fewer targeted abilities per stage); improved
413	psychological focus and motivation; more targeted nutrition per block (e.g., higher protein
414	during strength-focused blocks); and — most relevant to the peaking question — "a
415	multi-stage annual plan creates more favorable conditions for peaking in time for the main
416	competition of the season," with intermediate peaks plannable mid-season or even early
417	season, not only at a single season-end date.
418	
419	**Why it works** — Because each training stage runs its own compressed
420	accumulation-transmutation-realization cycle and ends in a real competitive test, the athlete
421	is brought to a peak (or near-peak) at the end of every stage rather than once per year;
422	stacking four to seven such stages across a season is what produces the multi-peak pattern.
423	Issurin's stated physiological contrast (Table 1.8) is that the traditional model relies on
424	adaptation to concurrent stimuli across a long period, while this model relies on
425	superimposing sequential residual effects from short, concentrated blocks — the same
426	mechanism underlying [[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]].
427	
428	**When to apply** — This is the entry most directly responsive to the strength-and-conditioning
429	miss-log gap ("peaking phase structure for collegiate football," logged 2026-09-03): for a
430	football program needing camp-readiness, then in-season week-to-week competitive readiness,
431	this framework suggests treating each significant test point (fall camp scrimmage, each
432	game week, or a defined in-season block) as a candidate training-stage boundary rather than
433	relying on a single annual peak, with the caveat below about untested claims. **Eric's
434	baseline** does not currently describe an explicit training-stage or multi-peak model for
435	football; the closest baseline material is the general macro/meso/microcycle planning
436	language and the in-season rule "maintain intensity, reduce volume" (`method-baseline.md`,
437	"Periodization and programming" and "Strength and power," citing
438	`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md` pp.17-18, 20-21) — this Issurin framework offers a
439	more explicit structural answer to "how do you actually sequence a season with more than one
440	peak" than anything currently captured in the baseline.
441	
442	**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — The "four to seven stages" and "about two months"
443	figures are stated without a derivation the reader can check — Issurin gives no worked
444	example of how stage count or duration is calculated for a specific sport's calendar in
445	this chapter. **Inference:** football's in-season structure (weekly games, not discrete
446	multi-week competition-free blocks) does not map cleanly onto a ~2-month training stage —
447	Issurin's model is built from and mainly evidenced by individual/dual sports with
448	discrete competitions (track and field, canoe-kayak, windsurfing), and Chapter 3's
449	microcycle-level material (not yet ingested; see `_book.md` for the recommended next batch)
450	is likely necessary before this framework can be translated into a week-by-week in-season
451	football plan. **Contested — flag as unqualified:** the "does not work well for
452	high-performance athletes" framing of the traditional alternative carries the same caveat as
453	in [[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]] — Bompa & Haff's 5th edition, already
454	in this library, is a current high-level training text that does not abandon
455	period-based (as opposed to stage-based) annual planning. **Inference:** Issurin's own 2016
456	review (Zotero item `PT9QTQ2I`, not yet full-text-cached) is titled around benefits *and*
457	limitations of block periodization and likely qualifies the confident five-benefit list
458	above; this entry's claims should be revisited once that review is read.
459	
460	**Example** — A five-stage football off-season/camp plan: Stage 1 (general
461	accumulation, ~8 weeks, winter conditioning); Stage 2 (strength/power transmutation into
462	spring ball, ending in the spring game as a "competition"); Stage 3 (summer accumulation);
463	Stage 4 (fall-camp transmutation, ending in the first scrimmage or game week as
464	realization); Stage 5+ (in-season stages keyed to bye weeks or rivalry-week peaks, pending
465	Chapter 3's in-season microcycle guidance).
466	
467	**Related** — [[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]],
468	[[claim--multi-peak-annual-preparation-elite-track-and-field]] (the empirical motivation for
469	needing a multi-peak model), [[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]],
470	[[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]].

## Schema

Follow `C:\Users\eric_rash\.claude\skills\ingest-book\SKILL.md` exactly: `_domain.md`, `_book.md` (map and resume checkpoint, updated after EACH chapter or unit), and entries named `<kind>--<kebab-slug>.md` with kind one of principle, framework, case-study, heuristic, claim. ## Voices: label every one

- **The source author's statements are plain text.**
- **Eric's views** (from `docs/method-baseline.md` or his reviews) are prefixed "Eric's baseline:" or "Eric's review:".
- **Your own reasoning, application or synthesis** is prefixed "Inference:".
- **Nothing unlabeled that the author did not say.** The most common failures: a judgment from Eric's review written as if the author said it; a mechanism the author never gave presented as "why it works" (write "The author gives no mechanism. Inference: ..."); an invented example.

## Lessons from the Supertraining Chapter 1 review (2026-09-26: 30 FIX, 1 NO-GO of 41)

- **Keep the source's internal contradictions.** When a book says X on one page and not-X on another, record both with their pages and set `contested`. Never pick one side silently. The NO-GO entry reversed the book's SJ-CMJ strength-deficit rule because the book states it both ways.
- **Name the right voice.** In co-authored books, write "the authors" unless a passage clearly belongs to one author. A passage that names Verkhoshansky in the third person is Siff writing.
- **Keep `proven` rare and scoped.** Scope it to the replicated core (for example, "Hill's force-velocity curve"), never the whole entry, and mark any disputed sentence inside it. Four of eight `proven` ratings were lowered.
- **No mechanism the source does not give.** About a dozen "Why it works" sections supplied physiology the book never states. Label it "Inference:" or leave it out.
- **Do not add "well established" or "modern research shows" without a citation.** Name the paper, or delete the phrase.

## Evidence

- Every number, definition and quote carries a checkable locator: PDF page (and printed page if it differs), or file plus timestamp. Never write "confirmed in PDF" unless you opened that page.
- Never invent a number. Keep ambiguity visible: mark unclear audio or OCR as unclear, and do not harmonize two conflicting numbers from the source; record both with their locators.
- OCR sources (`staging/ocr/*.md`): pages listed as low_confidence in the header must be checked against the page image before any number from them is cited. Use the Read tool on the PDF page, or render it.

## Confidence

- Practitioner courses and lectures: ceiling `supported`.
- Books: `proven` only for established, widely replicated physiology or mechanics. Soviet-era or single-lab empirical findings and training prescriptions: `supported` at most. `untested` for single cases and anecdotes. `contested` where another library source or modern evidence disagrees (say which).

Before each entry, grep `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\SecondBrain\Knowledge\library` and the staging library (`C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV\Flint\.claude\worktrees\step1-triage\staging\library`) for the concept. # Concentration of Training Workloads Is the Cornerstone Principle of Block Periodization

**What it is** — Issurin states the Block Periodization Concept (BPC) rests on one
foundational principle, concentration of training workloads, from which two others follow:
(1) a minimal number of targeted abilities per block, because highly concentrated loads
"only provide sufficient training stimuli to improve the targeted ability," and (2)
consecutive (not simultaneous) development of abilities, because "the number of decisive
abilities exceeds the number of abilities that can be developed simultaneously" (PDF p. 37,
printed p. 26, Figure 1.7). The rationale is laid out as a table of contradictions in the
traditional, simultaneous-development model for high-level athletes (Table 1.4, PDF p. 20,
printed p. 9): concurrent workloads compete for limited energy supply, differing
physiological-system restoration times leave athletes under-recovered for all targets at
once, workloads interact negatively (energy deficits, technical complexity, neuromuscular
fatigue), mental concentration cannot be split across many targets, and the training
stimulus needed for a high-level athlete's progress cannot be reached when it is divided
among many abilities.

**Why it works** — Issurin's own explanation is that above a threshold of athletic level,
a quality only responds to a training stimulus concentrated enough to exceed that
threshold; splitting the same total training time across many qualities keeps each one's
stimulus below that threshold. He does not give a quantitative mechanism for where that
threshold sits or how "concentrated enough" is defined for a given ability or athlete — the
principle is argued from coaches' and scientists' collective experience (Table 1.4) rather
than derived from a stated dose-response model.

**When to apply** — Designing training blocks for advanced, high-level athletes juggling
more qualities than can be trained well at once (the explicit target population, per
Issurin). **Eric's baseline:** this converges with the department's own compatibility rule,
"you can't ride two horses with one saddle" — incompatible qualities are not both trained at
full intensity in the same block (`method-baseline.md`, "Periodization and programming,"
citing `01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md` pp.28-29). It also converges with
[[periodization--bompa/principle--concentrated-loading-overreaching]], which independently
describes concentrated, saturated loading on one quality with a delayed 4-12 week rebound.

**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — Issurin's own text (PDF p. 44, printed p. 33) states the
traditional, complex (simultaneous multi-ability) model "has visible benefits for the
preparation of low- and mid-level athletes": it is "more diversified, attractive and
lively," and medium-level concentration is "sufficient stimulation" at that level — the
concentration principle is explicitly scoped to high-performance athletes, not a universal
programming rule. **Contested:** Issurin's blanket claim elsewhere in the same chapter that
the traditional model "does not work well for high-performance athletes" (PDF p. 19,
printed p. 8) is disputed by this library's own Bompa & Haff 5th-edition material
(`periodization--bompa`), which is a current (not 1984-vintage) textbook still teaching and
defending a form of the traditional/complex periodization model for high-level athletes.
Issurin's critique in this chapter names Bompa's *1984* edition specifically (PDF p. 13,
printed p. 2) as one of the texts that propagated the traditional model he is arguing
against — it is not a critique of the Bompa & Haff 5th edition already in this library,
which incorporates concentrated-loading and conjugated-sequence ideas closer to Issurin's
own. **Inference:** Issurin's own later peer-reviewed review (2016, *Sports Medicine*,
"Benefits and Limitations of Block Periodized Training Approaches," Zotero item
`PT9QTQ2I`, not yet full-text-cached in this ingest) is titled around limitations as well as
benefits and likely narrows this 2008 book's confident framing; treat the frontmatter
`confidence: contested` as applying specifically to the universal "traditional doesn't work
for high performers" claim, not to the narrower, self-limited concentration principle.

**Example** — A collegiate football strength staff trying to develop max strength,
aerobic capacity, alactic power, and technical skill acquisition all at full intensity in
the same 4-week block, per Table 1.4's logic, risks under-stimulating all four rather than
meaningfully improving any one; concentrating the block on 1-2 of them (with the rest held
at a retention dose) is the alternative Issurin argues for.

**Related** — [[framework--block-periodization-mesocycle-taxonomy]] — the three-block
structure this principle produces. [[periodization--bompa/principle--concentrated-loading-overreaching]]
and [[periodization--bompa/framework--step-loading-paradigm]] — converging concentrated-load
ideas already in this library. [[supertraining--verkhoshansky/principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]] (staging) —
check for overlap on why generalized simultaneous training under-delivers for advanced
athletes.

# No More Than Three Training Modalities Per Workout, With 65-70% of Time on One or Two

**What it is** — Issurin extends the concentration principle to single-session design
(Figure 2.4, PDF p. 75, printed p. 63; Table 2.12, PDF p. 76, printed p. 65) with five
stated rules (PDF p. 75, printed p. 64): (1) a workout should contain **no more than three
training modalities** — typically one dominant, one compatible with the main purpose, and
one for technique/tactics improvement or restoration; (2) **65-70% of total training time**
in a development workout should go to one or two selected modalities, to preserve workload
concentration; (3) after a key-workout, the following session should show a significant
load reduction — running two consecutive key-workouts is possible but risks excessive load
concentration; (4) hypertrophy-focused sessions require workload to be "substantially
reduced" for **at least 20 hours** afterward to protect the anabolic phase of muscle
restoration; (5) limiting modality count matters most in high-performance training —
junior/developmental athletes' programs can be more diverse and multilateral. Figure 2.4
maps which modalities are compatible as secondary/tertiary additions to five dominant ones:
aerobic endurance pairs with alactic sprint, strength-endurance-aerobic, and
hypertrophy-strength (placed after); anaerobic glycolytic endurance pairs with
strength-endurance-anaerobic, aerobic restoration, and mixed aerobic-anaerobic endurance;
alactic sprint pairs with aerobic endurance, explosive strength, hypertrophy-strength
(after), and aerobic restoration; hypertrophy-strength pairs with neural-strength, flexibility,
and aerobic restoration; new-technical-skill learning pairs with any modality, but only
*after* the dominant task. Table 2.12 gives the physiological/psychological rationale for
several of the strongest pairings (e.g., aerobic endurance + strength endurance: increased
oxidation supports the resistance work; alactic sprint + aerobic endurance: brief sprints
break monotony and keep a wide muscle-fiber pool activated for the subsequent aerobic work).

**Why it works — the specific numeric thresholds are asserted, not derived** — The
underlying logic is the same concentration principle from Chapter 1
([[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]]): splitting a session across too many
modalities dilutes the stimulus for all of them. **Inference:** Issurin gives no stated
derivation for why the cutoff is exactly three modalities rather than two or four, why the
time-share threshold is 65-70% rather than some other range, or why 20 hours is the specific
reduced-load window after hypertrophy work (versus, e.g., 24 or 48 hours) — these read as
the author's own practical rules of thumb built from coaching experience rather than
citations to a dose-response study.

**When to apply** — Auditing whether a practice plan or lift is trying to do too much:
count distinct training modalities in a session and check whether one or two of them
actually receive the majority of training time, per the 65-70% rule. Use Figure 2.4/Table
2.12 to check whether a planned secondary modality is a known-compatible pairing or an
unaddressed combination. **Eric's baseline** independently states a directionally identical
rule for compatibility, though at the block level rather than the single-session level:
"incompatible qualities... are not both targeted at full intensity in the same block"
(`method-baseline.md`, "Periodization and programming," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md` pp.28-29, "you can't ride two horses with one
saddle") — this Issurin entry gives that same instinct a specific numeric structure (≤3
modalities, 65-70% time-share) that the baseline material does not currently specify at
either the block or session level.

**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — Treat the ≤3-modality, 65-70%, and 20-hour figures as
Issurin's own heuristics rather than established constants — no citation or underlying data
is given for any of the three in this chapter. Issurin explicitly narrows the number
constraints to high-performance training; junior/developmental programming is stated to
reasonably need more variety, not fewer modalities. Figure 2.4's compatibility map is not
exhaustive (it covers five dominant modalities, not every possible combination) — an
untested pairing should not be assumed incompatible or compatible by default; Issurin gives
no guidance for modalities not shown in the figure.

**Example** — A practice plan combining strength-endurance, aerobic-anaerobic conditioning,
maximal-speed sprint work, and new-install technical work in one session would have four
distinct modalities, exceeding the stated ≤3 rule; per Figure 2.4, glycolytic endurance
pairs well with strength-endurance-anaerobic and aerobic restoration, but maximal speed and
new technical skill acquisition would need to be reduced to secondary/tertiary roles or
moved to a separate session to keep the session within the concentration guideline.

**Related** — [[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]],
[[heuristic--exercise-sequencing-by-fatigue-state]],
[[framework--key-workout-and-key-exercise-concept]].

# Accumulation, Transmutation (Transformation), and Realization: the Three Mesocycle-Blocks

**What it is** — Issurin's core structural unit is the mesocycle-block, one of three types
(Table 1.7, PDF p. 37, printed p. 26): **Accumulation** targets basic abilities (aerobic
endurance, muscular strength, basic coordination) with high volume/reduced intensity and
"reasonable restoration"; **Transmutation** targets sport-specific abilities (special
endurance, strength endurance, proper technique) with reduced volume/increased intensity,
and explicitly does *not* provide full restoration — fatigue accumulates; **Realization**
targets integrative, competition-ready preparedness (model performances, maximum speed,
event-specific tactics) at low-medium volume/high intensity, with full restoration required
going in. Each type has its own monitoring focus: basic-ability tests for accumulation,
sport-specific-ability tests for transmutation, and maximum speed/strategy checks for
realization. **Locator note:** the 1985 origin paper (Issurin & Kaverin) and this book's
1.2.1 narrative (PDF p. 33, printed p. 22) use the term **transformation**; from section
1.2.2 onward (PDF p. 37+, printed p. 26+) and in the book's own tables, the term used is
**transmutation**. Both names refer to the same middle block; record both because a search
for either term should resolve to this entry.

**Why it works** — The sequencing is designed to exploit the fact that different motor
abilities have different **residual training effect** durations (see
[[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]]): basic abilities (aerobic
endurance, max strength) decay slowest, so they can be built early and coast on their own
residual while transmutation and realization narrow the focus toward faster-decaying,
more specific and speed-dependent qualities close to competition. Issurin frames this as
superimposition of residual effects (Figure 1.8, PDF p. 39, printed p. 28) rather than
concurrent development of everything at once.

**When to apply** — Structuring a training stage (the accumulation-transmutation-realization
sequence, ending in competition) for advanced athletes who need multiple qualities peaked
together — see [[framework--training-stage-and-multi-peak-annual-cycle]] for how these three
blocks compose into a full annual plan. **Eric's baseline** shows a structurally similar but
independently-arrived-at sequence: the department's own preparatory-period design goes
hypertrophy/work-capacity, then basic strength, then strength-to-power
(`method-baseline.md`, "Periodization and programming," citing week1-lecture.md pp.43-48) —
a general-to-specific progression that parallels accumulation-to-realization, though the
baseline's sequence is not explicitly framed with Issurin's residual-effect superimposition
logic or his restoration-status distinctions between blocks.

**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — This is a three-way classification built for advanced
athletes who can tolerate the fatigue-accumulating transmutation block (see
[[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]] for the low-/mid-level-athlete
carve-out). It presumes a training stage that ends in a real competition or test date to
absorb the realization block's tapering logic; without a fixed target date, there is no
clear trigger for when accumulation should end and transmutation begin. **Contested (partly):**
the vault's Bompa & Haff material (`periodization--bompa/principle--concentrated-loading-overreaching`)
independently describes a comparable saturated-load-then-restitution structure with a
4-12 week delayed rebound — a longer and less rigidly three-staged model than Issurin's
roughly two-month training stage (below); the two should be read as convergent but not
identical prescriptions, and a program note should say which model's timing a given plan
follows.

**Example** — A training stage built for a mid-season peak: 3-4 weeks of accumulation
(aerobic base, general strength), 3-4 weeks of transmutation (sport-specific conditioning,
strength-endurance, technique under fatigue), then 1-2 weeks of realization (tapered
volume, high-intensity model-speed work, full restoration) ending at the target competition
or test date.

**Related** — [[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]],
[[framework--training-stage-and-multi-peak-annual-cycle]],
[[case-study--bondarchuk-hammer-throw-block-mesocycles]] (a different three-block taxonomy
from the same era, worth distinguishing from this one),
[[periodization--bompa/principle--concentrated-loading-overreaching]],
[[periodization--bompa/framework--step-loading-paradigm]].

# The Training Stage (A-T-R + Competition) Is the Annual Plan's Building Block, Enabling Multiple Peaks

**What it is** — Issurin's annual cycle is built from a sequence of **training stages**,
each one containing all three mesocycle-blocks (accumulation, transmutation, realization) in
order, ending in a competition (PDF p. 38, printed p. 27). Each training stage "gives the
appearance of an annual cycle in miniature" — a block resembling a preparatory period
(accumulation), one resembling a competition period (transmutation), and a tapering block
ending in competitive performance (realization) (PDF p. 39, printed p. 28). The duration of
a training stage is set by how long the constituent residual training effects can be
superimposed (Figure 1.8; see
[[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]]) and "should be about two
months," though Issurin notes stages can run shorter near season's end or longer earlier in
the season, in which case "special measures should be used to prolong residual training
effects" (unspecified in this chapter — likely developed in Chapter 3, not yet ingested).
The number of training stages in a season "usually varies from four to seven," depending on
the sport's competition calendar (PDF p. 40, printed p. 29, Figure 1.9). Issurin lists five
claimed benefits of this design over the traditional model (PDF p. 40, printed p. 29, and
Table 1.8, PDF p. 42, printed p. 31): reduced total training volume without reducing workout
count; more purposeful monitoring (fewer targeted abilities per stage); improved
psychological focus and motivation; more targeted nutrition per block (e.g., higher protein
during strength-focused blocks); and — most relevant to the peaking question — "a
multi-stage annual plan creates more favorable conditions for peaking in time for the main
competition of the season," with intermediate peaks plannable mid-season or even early
season, not only at a single season-end date.

**Why it works** — Because each training stage runs its own compressed
accumulation-transmutation-realization cycle and ends in a real competitive test, the athlete
is brought to a peak (or near-peak) at the end of every stage rather than once per year;
stacking four to seven such stages across a season is what produces the multi-peak pattern.
Issurin's stated physiological contrast (Table 1.8) is that the traditional model relies on
adaptation to concurrent stimuli across a long period, while this model relies on
superimposing sequential residual effects from short, concentrated blocks — the same
mechanism underlying [[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]].

**When to apply** — This is the entry most directly responsive to the strength-and-conditioning
miss-log gap ("peaking phase structure for collegiate football," logged 2026-09-03): for a
football program needing camp-readiness, then in-season week-to-week competitive readiness,
this framework suggests treating each significant test point (fall camp scrimmage, each
game week, or a defined in-season block) as a candidate training-stage boundary rather than
relying on a single annual peak, with the caveat below about untested claims. **Eric's
baseline** does not currently describe an explicit training-stage or multi-peak model for
football; the closest baseline material is the general macro/meso/microcycle planning
language and the in-season rule "maintain intensity, reduce volume" (`method-baseline.md`,
"Periodization and programming" and "Strength and power," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md` pp.17-18, 20-21) — this Issurin framework offers a
more explicit structural answer to "how do you actually sequence a season with more than one
peak" than anything currently captured in the baseline.

**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — The "four to seven stages" and "about two months"
figures are stated without a derivation the reader can check — Issurin gives no worked
example of how stage count or duration is calculated for a specific sport's calendar in
this chapter. **Inference:** football's in-season structure (weekly games, not discrete
multi-week competition-free blocks) does not map cleanly onto a ~2-month training stage —
Issurin's model is built from and mainly evidenced by individual/dual sports with
discrete competitions (track and field, canoe-kayak, windsurfing), and Chapter 3's
microcycle-level material (not yet ingested; see `_book.md` for the recommended next batch)
is likely necessary before this framework can be translated into a week-by-week in-season
football plan. **Contested — flag as unqualified:** the "does not work well for
high-performance athletes" framing of the traditional alternative carries the same caveat as
in [[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]] — Bompa & Haff's 5th edition, already
in this library, is a current high-level training text that does not abandon
period-based (as opposed to stage-based) annual planning. **Inference:** Issurin's own 2016
review (Zotero item `PT9QTQ2I`, not yet full-text-cached) is titled around benefits *and*
limitations of block periodization and likely qualifies the confident five-benefit list
above; this entry's claims should be revisited once that review is read.

**Example** — A five-stage football off-season/camp plan: Stage 1 (general
accumulation, ~8 weeks, winter conditioning); Stage 2 (strength/power transmutation into
spring ball, ending in the spring game as a "competition"); Stage 3 (summer accumulation);
Stage 4 (fall-camp transmutation, ending in the first scrimmage or game week as
realization); Stage 5+ (in-season stages keyed to bye weeks or rivalry-week peaks, pending
Chapter 3's in-season microcycle guidance).

**Related** — [[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]],
[[claim--multi-peak-annual-preparation-elite-track-and-field]] (the empirical motivation for
needing a multi-peak model), [[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]],
[[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]].

# A Morning Full-Body Resistance Workout Did Not Hurt Jump, Anaerobic Power, or Shooting Accuracy Six Hours Later

**What it is** — Woolstenhulme et al. (2004), cited by Issurin (PDF p. 80, printed p. 69):
highly trained female basketball players (ages 18-22; exact sample size not stated in this
text) completed a within-subject comparison on two separate days. On the experimental day,
they performed a full-body morning resistance workout (7 exercises, 3-6 sets, 5-12RM loads),
then after **six hours of rest** were tested on vertical jump, a 30-second Wingate anaerobic
cycling test, and a 60-second shooting-accuracy trial. On the control day, the same test
battery was completed without the preceding resistance workout. Statistical analysis found
no differences between the athletes' results on the experimental vs. control days. Issurin's
stated conclusion: "a high-resistance full-body workout of moderate intensity has no negative
impact on the manifestation of sport-specific athletic abilities of trained basketball
players after six hours of rest."

**Why it works — inference, not stated in the cited passage** — Six hours appears to be
sufficient for the acute neuromuscular fatigue from a moderate-intensity, moderate-volume
resistance session (5-12RM, 7 exercises) to resolve enough that it does not measurably
degrade jump, anaerobic power, or a skill-accuracy task; Issurin does not present the
physiological recovery mechanism in this passage beyond citing the outcome.

**When to apply** — Directly relevant to the common scheduling question in football and
other team sports (per Issurin's framing, PDF p. 79-80, printed pp. 68-69): whether morning
hours can be used for resistance training on a day with afternoon practice or competition,
given that in-season strength training is described elsewhere in this chapter as necessary
to offset the "dramatic losses of lean body mass, and maximum and explosive strength" a long
20-35 week competitive season can otherwise cause (Baker, 2001; Gamble, 2006, as cited by
Issurin, PDF pp. 79-80). This gives a specific, citable data point (six hours, moderate
5-12RM loading) supporting a same-day AM-lift/PM-practice-or-game model, consistent with
Eric's baseline's general in-season rule to "maintain intensity, reduce volume" rather than
avoid lifting in-season (`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md` pp.20-21).

**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — The cited sample is female basketball players; exact
sample size, loading specifics beyond "5-12RM," and effect-size/statistical detail are not
given in this text, so the finding should be treated as a directional result, not a precise
dosing guarantee. **Inference:** football involves substantially higher-impact,
higher-volume, and often heavier absolute loading than a 5-12RM "moderate intensity"
basketball-focused protocol, and involves collision-based rather than jump/shoot-accuracy
outcome measures — do not assume this six-hour window transfers unchanged to a heavier
football-specific lift or to contact-sport performance measures without independent
verification. The study also does not address multi-day accumulated fatigue from repeated
same-day lift-then-compete scheduling across a full season, only a single isolated
comparison day.

**Example** — A football program considering morning lifts on game day or heavy-practice
days has a citable data point that a moderate-intensity, moderate-volume full-body session
six hours before performance testing did not degrade jump, anaerobic power, or a
skill-accuracy measure in one studied population — but should treat football-specific
validation (heavier loads, contact-sport outcome measures) as a separate, unanswered
question.

**Related** — [[principle--training-modality-compatibility-in-a-workout]],
[[heuristic--two-a-day-workout-sequencing-by-dominant-ability]].

# World-Class Track and Field Athletes Compete and Peak Many Times Per Season, Not Once

**What it is** — Table 1.5 (PDF p. 24, printed p. 13, based on Suslov, 2001, with Issurin's
modifications) reports three world-class athletes' single-season competition patterns:
**Marion Jones** (100-200m, long jump; 1998 season) had **10 peaks** (8 in running, 2 in
long jump, all at personal-best level) across a **200-day** competitive span, with typical
19-22 day intervals between peaks. **Sergei Bubka** (pole vault; 1991 season) had **7
peaks** (all within 3% of his personal best, 595-612 cm) across a **265-day** span,
23-43 day intervals. **Stefka Kostadinova** (high jump; 1998 season) had **11 peaks** (all
within 3% of her personal best, 200-205 cm) across a combined **155-day** span (winter ~20
days; spring/summer 135 days), 14-25 day intervals. Issurin's summary point: these athletes'
5-8 month competitive spans "can not be subdivided into traditional preparatory and
competitive periods," yet their basic abilities (max strength, aerobic regeneration
capacity) still had to be maintained across that entire span.

**Why it works — this is observational, not interventional** — These are real competition
records for three specific, historically documented elite athletes (Olympic/World
champions), not an experiment; the "why" is a report of what elite competition calendars
actually looked like by 1991/1998, cited to Suslov's (2001) analysis rather than derived
from a controlled study of periodization models.

**When to apply** — As direct evidence for the strength-and-conditioning miss-log's
"peaking phase structure" gap: this table is the empirical case Issurin uses to argue that a
single annual peak (or even a two-/three-peak model) does not describe how modern elite
individual-sport athletes actually compete, which motivates the multi-stage annual model in
[[framework--training-stage-and-multi-peak-annual-cycle]]. Useful for framing the *problem*
(competition calendars now demand many peaks) to Baylor coaches even before the
*solution* (Chapter 3's microcycle-level guidance, not yet ingested) is available.

**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — All three examples are individual, non-contact,
technique/power sports (sprinting/jumping, pole vault, high jump) where "peak" can be defined
by a single measurable performance (time, height, distance) on a given day. **Inference:**
this evidence does not directly transfer to football, where "peak" is not a single
measurable output and the competitive calendar is fixed by a weekly game schedule rather
than a chosen sequence of meets — the multi-peak *problem* generalizes (a football season
also demands repeated high-level performance, not one), but the specific 19-43 day
inter-peak intervals shown here are specific to how often these particular athletes chose to
compete, not a transferable spacing rule for football practice or game weeks. Data source is
single (Suslov, 2001, "with modifications" by Issurin) with no stated method for how "peak"
was defined or verified for each performance.

**Example** — When explaining to a Baylor position group why in-season programming assumes
more than one readiness peak per season, this table is a citable, real-world existence proof
that elite athletes routinely peak 7-11 times in a season — useful for framing, not for
directly copying an inter-peak interval into a football in-season plan.

**Related** — [[framework--training-stage-and-multi-peak-annual-cycle]].

# Residual Training Effects Last Different Numbers of Days for Different Motor Abilities

**What it is** — The residual training effect is defined as "the retention of changes
induced by systematic workloads beyond a certain time period after the cessation of
training," a term Issurin attributes to Brian and James Counsilman (1991) (PDF p. 33,
printed p. 22). Issurin & Lustig (2004) is cited as the source of Table 1.6 (PDF p. 35,
printed p. 24), giving residual duration ± SD in days after cessation of training for each
motor ability: **aerobic endurance 30 ± 5 days**, **maximum strength 30 ± 5 days**,
**anaerobic glycolytic endurance 18 ± 4 days**, **strength endurance 15 ± 5 days**,
**maximum speed (alactic) 5 ± 3 days**. The stated physiological basis: aerobic endurance's
long residual rests on morphological/biochemical changes (aerobic enzymes, mitochondria,
capillaries, hemoglobin, glycogen storage) that increase 40-90% with training; maximum
strength's residual rests on comparably substantial morphological, biochemical and neural
changes (fiber cross-section, hyperplasia, motor-unit recruitment/synchronization,
motor-neuron discharge frequency, citing Zatsiorsky, 1995); maximum speed's short residual
reflects much smaller adaptations (phosphocreatine +2-5%, peak lactate +10-20%, anaerobic
enzymes +2-20%, citing Thorstensson, 1988) riding on delicate, unstable neuromuscular
patterns that decay quickly without continued training.

**Why it works — Inference** — Larger, more structural adaptations (aerobic
enzymatic/capillary changes, strength's neural and hypertrophic changes) persist longer
because the underlying tissue/enzyme changes take longer to reverse than the smaller,
more neurally-dependent changes behind peak speed. The author does not present this as an
experimentally isolated causal mechanism within this book — it is a physiological
rationale offered alongside the cited numbers, not derived from a controlled decay study
run on the same subjects who produced the durations.

**When to apply** — Sequencing which ability to develop first in a training stage (see
[[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]]): an ability with a long
residual (aerobic endurance, max strength) can be built early in accumulation and largely
coast through transmutation/realization without a maintenance dose, while an ability with a
short residual (max speed) needs re-exposure close to competition or its gain will be lost
before it is used. **Eric's baseline directly echoes half of this table:** "Training
residual effects set the retraining cadence: aerobic capacity and max strength both need
re-exposure roughly every 30 days; speed needs re-exposure roughly every 5 days or tissue
readiness for max-velocity work degrades" (`method-baseline.md`, "Periodization and
programming," citing `01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md` p.27) — this 30/30/5-day
pattern matches Issurin's 30±5 / 30±5 / 5±3 figures closely enough that it is very likely
this table (or a source repeating it) is the origin of that course-material claim, though
neither source cites the other directly, so this should be confirmed with Eric rather than
asserted as fact.

**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — Treat the numbers as a synthesized rule of thumb
(±5, ±4, ±5, ±3 day spreads are themselves wide relative to the means), not a precise
per-athlete clock; Issurin does not report the sample or method behind Issurin & Lustig
(2004) in this text, so the table's evidentiary base cannot be checked further from this
source alone. **Contested — flag this directly to Eric:** a *different* part of the same
baseline corpus states the opposite ordering for detraining rate: "The traits easiest to
build (aerobic) are lost fastest under detraining; the traits hardest to build
(alactic/speed) are lost slowest" (`method-baseline.md`, "Conditioning and energy systems,"
citing `class-4-2026.md` p.47). This flatly contradicts both this table (aerobic residual
is the *longest*, tied with strength, at 30±5 days, while alactic speed is the *shortest*
at 5±3 days) and the baseline's own class-1-transcript-sourced claim quoted above. Do not
harmonize these three data points — record all three with their locators and resolve with
Eric directly; this may reflect two different course sessions describing genuinely
different things (e.g., "detraining of an untrained quality" vs. "retention of a
peaked/tapered quality"), but that reconciliation is not stated anywhere in the corpus.
**Inference:** this table also converges with, but is not identical to, the vault's
Verkhoshansky-staging entry on heterochronic adaptation
([[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--heterochronic-biochemical-adaptation-sequence]],
staging), which describes a *different* mechanism (order of biochemical sub-processes
gained/lost) rather than absolute day-counts per motor ability — both describe
heterochronicity in de-training, but at different levels of description; do not treat them
as restating the same specific claim.

**Example** — In a training stage that opens with 4 weeks of accumulation (building
aerobic base and max strength) followed by 3 weeks of transmutation and 2 weeks of
realization, the aerobic and strength gains from accumulation are still within their ~30-day
residual window when realization begins, so they need no further direct stimulus — but if
maximum speed work is not re-introduced within about 5 days of the target competition, its
residual will have already decayed below peak by competition day.

**Related** — [[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]],
[[periodization--bompa/heuristic--fatigue-fitness-3to1-ratio]] (a ratio-based rule for
fatigue-vs-fitness decay, distinct from this table's absolute per-ability day counts —
cross-reference, do not conflate),
[[supertraining--verkhoshansky/framework--fitness-fatigue-modeling-and-taper-timing]] (staging),
[[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--heterochronic-biochemical-adaptation-sequence]] (staging).

# Key-Workouts and Key-Exercises Apply the Concentration Principle Inside a Single Session

**What it is** — Issurin extends the BPC concentration principle (see
[[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]]) down to the level of a single session.
A **key-workout** is the most important development session in a training cycle, focused on
the current main training emphasis (Table 2.5, PDF p. 56, printed p. 45): it targets the
cycle's most relevant abilities (usually one motor-fitness and one technique/tactics
target), demands focused athlete motivation and coach support, is timed for the athlete's
"best time" (adjusted to prior load but not overly fatigued), is loaded at a
substantial/large/extreme level, favors partnership/team-spirit organizational forms, and
requires thorough objective monitoring (chronometry, HR, blood lactate, video). New,

# Quantifying Workout Load on a 1-5 Scale, Mapped to Borg RPE Bands

**What it is** — Issurin presents a load-related workout classification built around three
functions: **development**, **retention**, and **restoration** (PDF p. 52, printed p. 41).
Table 2.3 (PDF p. 53, printed p. 42, based on Zatsiorsky 1995, modified by Issurin 2003)
quantifies this on a 1-5 scale using restoration time as the objective marker: restoration
level 1 (< 12 hours), retention level 2 (12-24 hours), development-substantial level 3
(24-48 hours), development-large level 4 (48-72 hours), development-extreme level 5
(> 72 hours). Because restoration-time-based classification does not fit every training type
well (Issurin notes coordination/neuro-emotional-stress workouts need less restoration time
than the scale implies), Table 2.4 (PDF p. 54, printed p. 43) offers a parallel mapping using
Borg's Rate of Perceived Exertion scale (Borg, 1973): RPE 6-11 (very-very-easy to
fairly-easy) = restoration; RPE 12-14 (slightly difficult) = retention; RPE 15-16
(difficult) = development-substantial; RPE 17-18 (very difficult) = development-large; RPE
19-20 (very-very difficult) = development-extreme.

**Why it works — inference on the underlying logic** — Restoration time and perceived
exertion are both proxies for how disruptive a session was to homeostasis; using either (or
both together) lets a coach assign every workout a comparable numeric load value even in
non-measurable sports (team sports, gymnastics), which Issurin identifies as the practical
payoff: "the load level of each workout can be quantified and expressed numerically" (PDF
p. 54, printed p. 43), enabling load-dependent categorization (development vs. retention vs.
restoration) across an entire training plan, not just isolated hard/easy labeling.

**When to apply** — Building a simple, athlete-reportable RPE-based load log for sports or
settings where objective physiological monitoring (HR, blood lactate) is not available for
every session; classifying a completed week of training after the fact into
development/retention/restoration proportions to check whether the intended block emphasis
(see [[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]]) was actually
delivered. **Eric's baseline** does not currently name Borg's RPE scale specifically, though
session-level subjective load tracking is philosophically consistent with the department's
general preference for practical, staff-sustainable monitoring tools over burdensome ones
(`method-baseline.md`, "Load monitoring and GPS," on why daily wellness surveys were
abandoned when athletes learned to game them) — RPE has its own well-documented gaming risk
that is not addressed anywhere in this Issurin chapter and should be treated as an open
question, not assumed solved.

**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — **The author gives no mechanism** for why these
specific RPE cut-points (11/12, 14/15, 16/17, 18/19) map to these specific restoration-time
bands rather than some other set of cut-points; both tables are presented as ready-made
scales without a validation study cited in this chapter. RPE is a subjective, athlete-reported
measure and is vulnerable to the same reporting-fatigue and gaming dynamics documented
elsewhere for subjective wellness tools; do not treat it as equivalent in reliability to the
objective HR/blood-lactate markers used in Table 2.10's key-exercise prescriptions
(see [[framework--key-workout-and-key-exercise-concept]]). The scale also does not
distinguish RPE driven by physical load from RPE driven by psychological/technical/cognitive
demand (e.g., a technically difficult but physically light session), a limitation Issurin
himself flags when noting coordination-heavy sessions need less restoration than their
subjective difficulty might imply.

players self-report session RPE, multiply by session duration (an approach not itself stated
in this chapter but a standard extension of Borg RPE elsewhere in sport science, noted here
as an inference, not something Issurin describes), and classify the week's development
vs. retention vs. restoration balance against the intended training-stage emphasis.

**Related** — [[framework--key-workout-and-key-exercise-concept]],
[[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]].

# A Morning Full-Body Resistance Workout Did Not Hurt Jump, Anaerobic Power, or Shooting Accuracy Six Hours Later

**What it is** — Woolstenhulme et al. (2004), cited by Issurin (PDF p. 80, printed p. 69):
highly trained female basketball players (ages 18-22; exact sample size not stated in this
text) completed a within-subject comparison on two separate days. On the experimental day,
they performed a full-body morning resistance workout (7 exercises, 3-6 sets, 5-12RM loads),
then after **six hours of rest** were tested on vertical jump, a 30-second Wingate anaerobic
cycling test, and a 60-second shooting-accuracy trial. On the control day, the same test
battery was completed without the preceding resistance workout. Statistical analysis found
no differences between the athletes' results on the experimental vs. control days. Issurin's
stated conclusion: "a high-resistance full-body workout of moderate intensity has no negative
impact on the manifestation of sport-specific athletic abilities of trained basketball
players after six hours of rest."

**Why it works — inference, not stated in the cited passage** — Six hours appears to be
sufficient for the acute neuromuscular fatigue from a moderate-intensity, moderate-volume
resistance session (5-12RM, 7 exercises) to resolve enough that it does not measurably
degrade jump, anaerobic power, or a skill-accuracy task; Issurin does not present the
physiological recovery mechanism in this passage beyond citing the outcome.

**When to apply** — Directly relevant to the common scheduling question in football and
other team sports (per Issurin's framing, PDF p. 79-80, printed pp. 68-69): whether morning
hours can be used for resistance training on a day with afternoon practice or competition,
given that in-season strength training is described elsewhere in this chapter as necessary
to offset the "dramatic losses of lean body mass, and maximum and explosive strength" a long
20-35 week competitive season can otherwise cause (Baker, 2001; Gamble, 2006, as cited by
Issurin, PDF pp. 79-80). This gives a specific, citable data point (six hours, moderate
5-12RM loading) supporting a same-day AM-lift/PM-practice-or-game model, consistent with
Eric's baseline's general in-season rule to "maintain intensity, reduce volume" rather than
avoid lifting in-season (`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md` pp.20-21).

**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — The cited sample is female basketball players; exact
sample size, loading specifics beyond "5-12RM," and effect-size/statistical detail are not
given in this text, so the finding should be treated as a directional result, not a precise
dosing guarantee. **Inference:** football involves substantially higher-impact,
higher-volume, and often heavier absolute loading than a 5-12RM "moderate intensity"
basketball-focused protocol, and involves collision-based rather than jump/shoot-accuracy
outcome measures — do not assume this six-hour window transfers unchanged to a heavier
football-specific lift or to contact-sport performance measures without independent
verification. The study also does not address multi-day accumulated fatigue from repeated
same-day lift-then-compete scheduling across a full season, only a single isolated
comparison day.

**Example** — A football program considering morning lifts on game day or heavy-practice
days has a citable data point that a moderate-intensity, moderate-volume full-body session
six hours before performance testing did not degrade jump, anaerobic power, or a
skill-accuracy measure in one studied population — but should treat football-specific
validation (heavier loads, contact-sport outcome measures) as a separate, unanswered
question.

**Related** — [[principle--training-modality-compatibility-in-a-workout]],
[[heuristic--two-a-day-workout-sequencing-by-dominant-ability]].

# World-Class Track and Field Athletes Compete and Peak Many Times Per Season, Not Once

**What it is** — Table 1.5 (PDF p. 24, printed p. 13, based on Suslov, 2001, with Issurin's
modifications) reports three world-class athletes' single-season competition patterns:
**Marion Jones** (100-200m, long jump; 1998 season) had **10 peaks** (8 in running, 2 in
long jump, all at personal-best level) across a **200-day** competitive span, with typical
19-22 day intervals between peaks. **Sergei Bubka** (pole vault; 1991 season) had **7
peaks** (all within 3% of his personal best, 595-612 cm) across a **265-day** span,
23-43 day intervals. **Stefka Kostadinova** (high jump; 1998 season) had **11 peaks** (all
within 3% of her personal best, 200-205 cm) across a combined **155-day** span (winter ~20
days; spring/summer 135 days), 14-25 day intervals. Issurin's summary point: these athletes'
5-8 month competitive spans "can not be subdivided into traditional preparatory and
competitive periods," yet their basic abilities (max strength, aerobic regeneration
capacity) still had to be maintained across that entire span.

**Why it works — this is observational, not interventional** — These are real competition
records for three specific, historically documented elite athletes (Olympic/World
champions), not an experiment; the "why" is a report of what elite competition calendars
actually looked like by 1991/1998, cited to Suslov's (2001) analysis rather than derived
from a controlled study of periodization models.

**When to apply** — As direct evidence for the strength-and-conditioning miss-log's
"peaking phase structure" gap: this table is the empirical case Issurin uses to argue that a
single annual peak (or even a two-/three-peak model) does not describe how modern elite
individual-sport athletes actually compete, which motivates the multi-stage annual model in
[[framework--training-stage-and-multi-peak-annual-cycle]]. Useful for framing the *problem*
(competition calendars now demand many peaks) to Baylor coaches even before the
*solution* (Chapter 3's microcycle-level guidance, not yet ingested) is available.

**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — All three examples are individual, non-contact,
technique/power sports (sprinting/jumping, pole vault, high jump) where "peak" can be defined
by a single measurable performance (time, height, distance) on a given day. **Inference:**
this evidence does not directly transfer to football, where "peak" is not a single
measurable output and the competitive calendar is fixed by a weekly game schedule rather
than a chosen sequence of meets — the multi-peak *problem* generalizes (a football season
also demands repeated high-level performance, not one), but the specific 19-43 day
inter-peak intervals shown here are specific to how often these particular athletes chose to
compete, not a transferable spacing rule for football practice or game weeks. Data source is
single (Suslov, 2001, "with modifications" by Issurin) with no stated method for how "peak"
was defined or verified for each performance.

**Example** — When explaining to a Baylor position group why in-season programming assumes
more than one readiness peak per season, this table is a citable, real-world existence proof
that elite athletes routinely peak 7-11 times in a season — useful for framing, not for
directly copying an inter-peak interval into a football in-season plan.

**Related** — [[framework--training-stage-and-multi-peak-annual-cycle]].

# Residual Training Effects Last Different Numbers of Days for Different Motor Abilities

**What it is** — The residual training effect is defined as "the retention of changes
induced by systematic workloads beyond a certain time period after the cessation of
training," a term Issurin attributes to Brian and James Counsilman (1991) (PDF p. 33,
printed p. 22). Issurin & Lustig (2004) is cited as the source of Table 1.6 (PDF p. 35,
printed p. 24), giving residual duration ± SD in days after cessation of training for each
motor ability: **aerobic endurance 30 ± 5 days**, **maximum strength 30 ± 5 days**,
**anaerobic glycolytic endurance 18 ± 4 days**, **strength endurance 15 ± 5 days**,
**maximum speed (alactic) 5 ± 3 days**. The stated physiological basis: aerobic endurance's
long residual rests on morphological/biochemical changes (aerobic enzymes, mitochondria,
capillaries, hemoglobin, glycogen storage) that increase 40-90% with training; maximum
strength's residual rests on comparably substantial morphological, biochemical and neural
changes (fiber cross-section, hyperplasia, motor-unit recruitment/synchronization,
motor-neuron discharge frequency, citing Zatsiorsky, 1995); maximum speed's short residual
reflects much smaller adaptations (phosphocreatine +2-5%, peak lactate +10-20%, anaerobic
enzymes +2-20%, citing Thorstensson, 1988) riding on delicate, unstable neuromuscular
patterns that decay quickly without continued training.

**Why it works — Inference** — Larger, more structural adaptations (aerobic
enzymatic/capillary changes, strength's neural and hypertrophic changes) persist longer
because the underlying tissue/enzyme changes take longer to reverse than the smaller,
more neurally-dependent changes behind peak speed. The author does not present this as an
experimentally isolated causal mechanism within this book — it is a physiological
rationale offered alongside the cited numbers, not derived from a controlled decay study
run on the same subjects who produced the durations.

**When to apply** — Sequencing which ability to develop first in a training stage (see
[[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]]): an ability with a long
residual (aerobic endurance, max strength) can be built early in accumulation and largely
coast through transmutation/realization without a maintenance dose, while an ability with a
short residual (max speed) needs re-exposure close to competition or its gain will be lost
before it is used. **Eric's baseline directly echoes half of this table:** "Training
residual effects set the retraining cadence: aerobic capacity and max strength both need
re-exposure roughly every 30 days; speed needs re-exposure roughly every 5 days or tissue
readiness for max-velocity work degrades" (`method-baseline.md`, "Periodization and
programming," citing `01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md` p.27) — this 30/30/5-day
pattern matches Issurin's 30±5 / 30±5 / 5±3 figures closely enough that it is very likely
this table (or a source repeating it) is the origin of that course-material claim, though
neither source cites the other directly, so this should be confirmed with Eric rather than
asserted as fact.

**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — Treat the numbers as a synthesized rule of thumb
(±5, ±4, ±5, ±3 day spreads are themselves wide relative to the means), not a precise
per-athlete clock; Issurin does not report the sample or method behind Issurin & Lustig
(2004) in this text, so the table's evidentiary base cannot be checked further from this
source alone. **Contested — flag this directly to Eric:** a *different* part of the same
baseline corpus states the opposite ordering for detraining rate: "The traits easiest to
build (aerobic) are lost fastest under detraining; the traits hardest to build
(alactic/speed) are lost slowest" (`method-baseline.md`, "Conditioning and energy systems,"
citing `class-4-2026.md` p.47). This flatly contradicts both this table (aerobic residual
is the *longest*, tied with strength, at 30±5 days, while alactic speed is the *shortest*
at 5±3 days) and the baseline's own class-1-transcript-sourced claim quoted above. Do not
harmonize these three data points — record all three with their locators and resolve with
Eric directly; this may reflect two different course sessions describing genuinely
different things (e.g., "detraining of an untrained quality" vs. "retention of a
peaked/tapered quality"), but that reconciliation is not stated anywhere in the corpus.
**Inference:** this table also converges with, but is not identical to, the vault's
Verkhoshansky-staging entry on heterochronic adaptation
([[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--heterochronic-biochemical-adaptation-sequence]],
staging), which describes a *different* mechanism (order of biochemical sub-processes
gained/lost) rather than absolute day-counts per motor ability — both describe
heterochronicity in de-training, but at different levels of description; do not treat them
as restating the same specific claim.

**Example** — In a training stage that opens with 4 weeks of accumulation (building
aerobic base and max strength) followed by 3 weeks of transmutation and 2 weeks of
realization, the aerobic and strength gains from accumulation are still within their ~30-day
residual window when realization begins, so they need no further direct stimulus — but if
maximum speed work is not re-introduced within about 5 days of the target competition, its
residual will have already decayed below peak by competition day.

**Related** — [[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]],
[[periodization--bompa/heuristic--fatigue-fitness-3to1-ratio]] (a ratio-based rule for
fatigue-vs-fitness decay, distinct from this table's absolute per-ability day counts —
cross-reference, do not conflate),
[[supertraining--verkhoshansky/framework--fitness-fatigue-modeling-and-taper-timing]] (staging),
[[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--heterochronic-biochemical-adaptation-sequence]] (staging).
