p. 54, printed p. 43), enabling load-dependent categorization (development vs. retention vs.
restoration) across an entire training plan, not just isolated hard/easy labeling.

**When to apply** — Building a simple, athlete-reportable RPE-based load log for sports or
settings where objective physiological monitoring (HR, blood lactate) is not available for
every session; classifying a completed week of training after the fact into
development/retention/restoration proportions to check whether the intended block emphasis
(see [[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]]) was actually
delivered. **Eric's baseline** does not currently name Borg's RPE scale specifically, though
session-level subjective load tracking is philosophically consistent with the department's
general preference for practical, staff-sustainable monitoring tools over burdensome ones
(`method-baseline.md`, "Load monitoring and GPS," on why daily wellness surveys were
abandoned when athletes learned to game them) — RPE has its own well-documented gaming risk
that is not addressed anywhere in this Issurin chapter and should be treated as an open
question, not assumed solved.

**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — **The author gives no mechanism** for why these
specific RPE cut-points (11/12, 14/15, 16/17, 18/19) map to these specific restoration-time
bands rather than some other set of cut-points; both tables are presented as ready-made
scales without a validation study cited in this chapter. RPE is a subjective, athlete-reported
measure and is vulnerable to the same reporting-fatigue and gaming dynamics documented
elsewhere for subjective wellness tools; do not treat it as equivalent in reliability to the
objective HR/blood-lactate markers used in Table 2.10's key-exercise prescriptions
(see [[framework--key-workout-and-key-exercise-concept]]). The scale also does not
distinguish RPE driven by physical load from RPE driven by psychological/technical/cognitive
demand (e.g., a technically difficult but physically light session), a limitation Issurin
himself flags when noting coordination-heavy sessions need less restoration than their
subjective difficulty might imply.

**Example** — A coach without force-plate or HR-monitor access for every practice can have
players self-report session RPE, multiply by session duration (an approach not itself stated
in this chapter but a standard extension of Borg RPE elsewhere in sport science, noted here
as an inference, not something Issurin describes), and classify the week's development
vs. retention vs. restoration balance against the intended training-stage emphasis.

**Related** — [[framework--key-workout-and-key-exercise-concept]],
[[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]].

# Case Study: Bondarchuk's Developmental/Competitive/Restorative Blocks and the 1988 Hammer Throw Podium

**What it is** — Issurin credits Anatoly Bondarchuk, hammer-throw coach, with one of the
precursor systems to Block Periodization (PDF p. 32, printed p. 21). Based on his own
athletic career (1972 Olympic hammer-throw champion) and doctoral research on throwers'
training programs (1988), Bondarchuk built a periodization chart using three types of
specialized mesocycle-blocks: **developmental** (workload gradually increases to maximum),
**competitive** (load stabilizes, athletes focus on competitive performance), and
**restorative** (active recovery, preparing for the next developmental block). Stated
durations: developmental and competitive blocks are "usually four weeks," restorative "can
be shortened to two weeks." Sequencing depends on the competition schedule and individual
athlete response. The claimed outcome: Bondarchuk coached the gold, silver, and bronze
medalists in hammer throw at the 1988 Olympics — "the entire Olympic podium occupied by
athletes of the same coach" (Bondarchuk, 1986 and 1988, as cited by Issurin).

**Why it works — the author gives no mechanism beyond the general BPC rationale** —
Issurin does not describe Bondarchuk's own stated reasoning for why these particular block
lengths (4/4/2 weeks) or this particular three-way split (by competitive readiness rather
than by ability type) were chosen; the mechanism offered is the same general BPC logic
(concentrated, sequenced blocks beat simultaneous multi-ability training) applied
retroactively to Bondarchuk's design.

**When to apply — untested, use as a historical precedent, not as evidence** — Useful for
explaining the lineage of block-periodization thinking (Bondarchuk predates and directly
inspired Issurin's own accumulation/transmutation/realization taxonomy, per PDF p. 32-33)
and as an alternative three-block naming scheme organized around competitive readiness
(developmental/competitive/restorative) rather than ability type
(accumulation/transmutation/realization) — worth distinguishing the two schemes explicitly
when citing "Bondarchuk's blocks" versus "Issurin's blocks."

**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — This is a single coach's single-event outcome (n = 1
coaching program, one Olympic final) with no comparison group, no report of what other
finalists' training looked like, and total reliance on the coach's and Issurin's own
secondary account rather than an independent case audit. A three-medal sweep at one Olympics
is a striking result but cannot isolate the training design's contribution from athlete
talent, competitor variance on the day, or other coaching factors. Do not cite this as
evidence that a 4/4/2-week block cadence "works" for hammer throw or any other event; it
illustrates a design, not a validated dose-response finding. This is distinct from and
should not be merged with Issurin's own accumulation/transmutation/realization taxonomy — see
[[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]] for that separate, though
historically related, three-block system.

**Example** — A coach citing "block periodization has a track record" should specify
which system (Bondarchuk's competitive-readiness blocks or Issurin's ability-type blocks) and
should not present the 1988 podium sweep as generalizable evidence beyond "one documented
historical instance this concept coincided with a strong outcome."

**Related** — [[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]],
[[case-study--issurin-kaverin-canoe-kayak-block-periodization]] — a comparable single-coach
case from the same era; consider also cross-referencing
`fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer/framework--sprint-exercise-classes-bondarchuk-four-categories.md`
(vault) — the *same* coach (Bondarchuk), but a completely different, unrelated framework
of his (an exercise-classification taxonomy by movement similarity, not a mesocycle-timing
system). The two should never be conflated when either is cited.

# Two Studies Issurin Cites Against Simultaneous Development: Swimmer Interference and Kayaker Decay

**What it is** — Issurin presents two data-backed examples as motivation for abandoning
simultaneous multi-ability training (traditional periodization) in favor of consecutive,
concentrated blocks.

**(1) Swimmer concurrent-training interference (PDF pp. 21-22, printed pp. 10-11, Figure
1.3).** High-level male swimmers were studied over an 8-week early-season program combining
extensive swimming with resistive/power dry-land work aimed at swim-specific strength
(9-11 workouts/week; sample size not stated in this text). Measured: maximal force of
tethered swimming (Ftsw), dry-land explosive strength (Fexp), and dry-land strength
endurance (SE). Result: strength endurance improved markedly; swim-specific strength did not
improve; explosive strength *decreased* — despite about 30% of dry-land program time devoted
to maximal/explosive strength work. Issurin's mechanistic explanation: extensive endurance
work captures the metabolic (anabolic) energy needed for the hypertrophy and neural-drive
adaptations that explosive/maximal strength require, and the resulting chronic fatigue keeps
central and peripheral neural factors from the state needed for strength gains
(citing Klausen, 1990, for the neural-mechanism point).

**(2) Kayaker decay under traditional periodization (PDF p. 25-26, printed pp. 14-15,
Figure 1.4 — the in-text citation reads "Fig.1.3," which appears to be a labeling error in
the source; the described variables match Figure 1.4's caption, not Figure 1.3's).** A group
of highly qualified kayakers were tracked across a full annual cycle built on the classical
model (Issurin et al., 1986). Measured: mean distance velocity (Vd), velocity at anaerobic
threshold (V-AT), peak paddle force (PF), stroke rate (SR), muscle mass (MM). Result: the
long general-preparatory period raised V-AT, muscle mass and peak force substantially; but
during the extended, highly specialized competitive period, extensive aerobic work and
maximum-strength work were reduced or dropped as "harmful for racing technique," and V-AT,
peak force, and muscle mass all *declined* by the competitive period. Distance velocity
still reached its season maximum, but only via increased stroke rate compensating for
reduced force — i.e., technique/rate covered for a real loss in the underlying strength and
aerobic qualities. Issurin's summary: "the timing pattern for developing different abilities
was far from optimal."

**Why it works** — For the swimmer case, Issurin's own stated mechanism is that extensive
endurance work "captures the metabolic energy that is necessary for anabolism during
post-exercise recovery," suppressing the muscle hypertrophy and neural-drive adaptations
strength training requires, and that chronic fatigue from high-volume training keeps
"central and peripheral neural factors... far from optimum" (PDF pp. 21-22, printed pp.
10-11, citing Klausen, 1990, for the neural-mechanism point). For the kayaker case, Issurin
gives no physiological mechanism for the decline beyond narration of what happened (reduced
aerobic and strength work during the competitive period, PDF p. 25, printed p. 14) — treat
that case as a described pattern, not an explained one. **Inference:** labeling the two
cases as "concurrent interference" versus "sequential decay" is this entry's own
categorization for cross-referencing purposes, not language Issurin himself uses; both are
offered by Issurin as evidence for the same underlying argument against simultaneous,
non-block training (see [[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]]), which in turn
motivates the consecutive block sequencing in
[[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]] and
[[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]].

**When to apply** — The swimmer study is the stronger evidence of the two: it is a
controlled, measured 8-week study with named outcome variables, giving concrete numbers
useful for illustrating concurrent-training interference to Baylor strength staff
programming for athletes who need both an aerobic base and explosive/max strength (e.g.,
many football positions in a fall-camp conditioning window). The kayaker case is useful
mainly as a cautionary illustration of "building a quality early in the year and then
letting it decay unaddressed."

**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — The swimmer study's exact sample size is not given in
this text (only workout frequency, 9-11/week), so its statistical strength cannot be judged
from this source alone — treat the direction of the finding (interference occurred) as
`supported` but the specific numeric changes in Figure 1.3 as unverifiable without the
original 1986/whichever-year source Issurin drew Figure 1.3 from (not cited by name on this
page). **Untested:** the kayaker case is Issurin's own team's data (Issurin et al., 1986),
observational across one season with no control group — it demonstrates a plausible pattern,
not a controlled comparison against an alternative periodization model run on the same
athletes. Neither study is football-specific; football's in-season structure (weekly
competition, not one late-season peak) differs from both the swimmers' fixed 8-week block and
the kayakers' single annual peak design.

**Example** — A Baylor position group with both an in-season conditioning demand and a
strength-maintenance demand should treat "just add more of both" as the swimmer study's
failure mode: without deliberate sequencing or volume management, the concurrent aerobic
load can blunt the intended strength/power adaptation even when strength work is
programmed.

**Related** — [[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]] (Table 1.4's rationale,
which these two studies are offered as concrete illustrations of),
[[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]].

# Case Study: The USSR Canoe-Kayak Team and the Original Accumulation/Transmutation/Realization Design

**What it is** — Issurin's own account of where his accumulation-transmutation-realization
taxonomy came from (PDF p. 33, printed p. 22): in the early 1980s, elite USSR canoe-kayak
paddlers were training an "enormous exercise volume" that the author and colleagues judged
excessive. The block-and-mesocycle-sequencing idea was "conceptualized, implemented and
proved in practice" with the national team, then published (Issurin & Kaverin, 1985). The
modified design allowed "about a 10-15% reduction in the annual training volume." Follow-up
testing during preparation reportedly showed "considerable improvement in the main fitness
components in all subgroups." The claimed competitive outcomes: three gold and three silver
medals at the 1988 Seoul Olympics, and eight gold medals (1989) and nine gold medals (1990)
at the World Championships.

**Why it works — the author's own interpretation, not independently verified here** —
Issurin attributes the improvement to reduced simultaneous multi-ability training and better
volume management under the new block structure, consistent with the general BPC rationale
in [[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]]. No comparison data (e.g., what the
same team's results looked like in prior Olympic/World Championship cycles under the old
model, or what other nations' medal counts did over the same period) is presented in this
chapter to isolate the training-design change from other factors (athlete development,
equipment, competitor turnover).

**When to apply — untested, treat as the concept's origin story, not as proof** — Useful
as the direct provenance of Issurin's own taxonomy (see
[[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]]) and as a data point that a
national federation with centralized, well-resourced athlete monitoring implemented this
design at scale (not just with one athlete).

**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — This is the concept's inventor reporting on his own
uncontrolled intervention with his own national team, published by the same author (Issurin
& Kaverin, 1985) — the account here (2008 book) is a secondary retelling with no cited
independent replication or outcome audit. As with the Bondarchuk case, do not treat the
Olympic and World Championship medal counts as a controlled test of the training design;
1980s Soviet sport had structural advantages (centralized athlete development, resourcing)
that are not present in most other training contexts, including a US college football
program. The "10-15% volume reduction" figure has no comparison baseline stated (reduction
from what specific prior volume, over what specific prior period) beyond "the annual
training volume."

**Example** — Citing "block periodization produced Olympic medals" should specify this is
one 1980s Soviet national-team case reported by the method's own originator, not a
controlled trial, and should be paired with the caveat already logged in
[[case-study--bondarchuk-hammer-throw-block-mesocycles]] about single-coach, single-program
evidence.

**Related** — [[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]],
[[case-study--bondarchuk-hammer-throw-block-mesocycles]].

# Squat-First vs. Squat-After-Hang-Pull Changes Whether You Get More Reps or More Power

**What it is** — Spreuwenberg et al. (2006), cited by Issurin (PDF p. 73, printed p. 62):
**nine** resistance-trained male athletes performed the back squat (4 sets at 85% of 1RM) on
two separate days under two protocols. Protocol A: squat performed during the initial part
of the workout. Protocol B: squat performed after a whole-body resistance exercise (hang
pull). Results: Protocol A produced significantly more repetitions per set (8.0 ± 1.9 vs.
5.4 ± 2.7 in Protocol B), but average power per set was *higher* in Protocol B. Issurin
attributes the power difference to postactivation potentiation induced by the preceding
whole-body power exercise.

**Why it works** — Issurin reports only the study authors' own attribution for the power
finding: they "attributed this phenomenon to postactivation potentiation induced by the
preceding whole-body power exercise" (PDF p. 73, printed p. 62). **Inference:** the
companion explanation for the rep-count finding, that fresh (unfatigued) muscle sustains
more total repetitions at a given relative load than muscle that has just performed a
preceding whole-body lift, is this entry's own reasoning to account for the Protocol A
result; Issurin does not state that explanation for the rep-count difference in this
passage.

**When to apply** — Choosing exercise order based on the specific training goal for that
session: Issurin's stated takeaway (PDF p. 73, printed p. 62) is that a coach wanting maximum
hypertrophy stimulus should place the squat early in the session (more total volume/reps),
while a coach targeting maximum power output should place it after appropriate whole-body
resistance work, to exploit postactivation potentiation. Directly usable for Baylor
strength-staff session design when max-effort lower-body power output (not volume) is the
stated goal of a given lift.

**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — This is a small (n = 9), single published study;
Issurin does not report effect sizes, statistical significance values, or the specific
whole-body exercise's loading in this citation beyond "hang pull" — treat the direction of
the finding as `supported` but do not treat the exact magnitude (8.0 vs. 5.4 reps) as
something to replicate precisely without reading the original study. It is unclear from this
text whether the postactivation-potentiation effect generalizes to different athlete
populations (this sample was resistance-trained males), different preceding exercises, or
different rest intervals between the potentiating exercise and the squat.

**Example** — A power-focused lower-body day for football linemen might sequence a
moderate-load hang pull or clean pull before back squats at 85% 1RM, accepting fewer total
squat reps in exchange for higher power output per rep on the squats that follow — a
hypertrophy-focused day for the same lift would instead put the squat first.

**Related** — [[heuristic--exercise-sequencing-by-fatigue-state]],
[[principle--training-modality-compatibility-in-a-workout]].

# A Structured Warm-Up/Cool-Down Program Cut Soccer Injuries Roughly Four-Fold Over Six Months

**What it is** — Ekstrand et al. (1983), cited by Issurin (PDF p. 58, printed p. 47,
Figure 2.1): **twelve** national-division soccer teams (**180 players**) were split into two
groups. The intervention group (six teams) used a modified program with carefully structured
warm-ups (ball exercises plus a stretching program) and cool-downs (jogging plus hold-relax
stretching), supervised by doctors and physiotherapists. The control group (six teams)
trained traditionally. Over a six-month follow-up, the intervention group showed "highly
significant superiority": a roughly **four-fold reduction in the number of injuries** and a
"drastic decrease" in workouts and games missed to musculoskeletal disorders. Issurin
separately cites supporting single-factor findings: stretching in warm-up increases lower
extremity range of motion in soccer players (Moller et al., 1985); active warm-up *without*
stretching does not affect flexibility (Zakas et al., 2006); and intense prior exercise
meaningfully stimulates aerobic metabolism in working muscles during subsequent strenuous
performance (Bangsbo et al., 2001). A related study (Moller et al., 1985, PDF p. 68, printed
p. 57) tracked 48 adult soccer players across three warm-up/cool-down protocols and found
that inserting a stretching series into the *cool-down* (not just the warm-up) produced range-
of-motion benefits both immediately after the session and 24 hours later, while stretching
only in the warm-up helped immediately but not at 24 hours.

**Why it works** — Issurin frames warm-up and cool-down as serving three functions each:
metabolic adjustment, technical/coordination adjustment, and mental readiness (warm-up,
Table 2.6, PDF p. 60, printed p. 49); and reduction of body temperature/HR/blood pressure,
removal of metabolic byproducts, endocrine-system recovery, and reduced emotional tension
(cool-down, Table 2.11, PDF p. 69, printed p. 58). **Contested — flag directly:** Issurin's
cool-down rationale explicitly frames blood lactate and "other acid metabolites" as "waste
products" to be "removed" from the muscles (PDF p. 68-69, printed pp. 57-58), citing a
specific clearance kinetic (blood lactate removal after a 4-minute exhausting time trial
takes about 20 minutes, Juel et al., 1990). This is in tension with a modern-physiology
claim already captured in this library's Verkhoshansky staging
([[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--lactate-and-oxygen-debt-myths]], `proven`): lactate is
not a toxin causing soreness or requiring active "removal," and it clears from the blood on
its own within about an hour of strenuous exercise regardless of cool-down activity, with
current research attributing post-exercise soreness to muscle/connective-tissue microtrauma
rather than residual lactate. The specific clearance-time citation (20 minutes for a 4-minute
time trial) may still be a real kinetic fact — that is not itself disputed here — but
Issurin's *framing* of this as evidence that cool-down actively "removes" a harmful waste
product reflects the outdated "lactic acid as toxin" model the Verkhoshansky entry corrects.
Cite this book's clearance-time number without repeating its waste-product framing.

**When to apply** — The Ekstrand et al. (1983) result is directly relevant to Applied
Performance's collaboration with Athletic Medicine on injury reduction: a structured,
medically-supervised warm-up/cool-down protocol is associated with a large, measured
reduction in soft-tissue injury incidence in a team sport, over a real six-month season, not
an acute lab measure. The cool-down-stretching timing finding (Moller et al., 1985) suggests
cool-down, not just warm-up, is where a stretching series may do more for next-day range of
motion.

**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — This is an observational, non-randomized team-level
comparison (teams chose or were assigned to conditions; individual randomization is not
described), and the intervention bundled multiple changes at once (warm-up content, cool-down
content, and medical/physiotherapy supervision), so the four-fold injury reduction cannot be
attributed to warm-up or cool-down alone — Issurin himself flags this study as "atypical
because it refers to the complex effects of warming-up, cooling-down and medical supervision"
(PDF p. 58, printed p. 47). **Contested:** stretching's effect on preventing delayed-onset
muscle soreness specifically is described by Issurin himself as disputed within this same
chapter — "supported by several studies (Hartfield, 1985) and contradicted by others (High
et al., 1989)" (PDF p. 70, printed p. 59) — do not cite stretching-prevents-DOMS as settled.

**Example** — A Baylor position group's practice-ending routine that pairs light locomotion
with a stretching series (rather than stretching only in the pre-practice warm-up) has some
support here for next-day range-of-motion benefit, though the causal strength of the
underlying Moller et al. (1985) study for injury outcomes specifically (as opposed to ROM)
is not established by this citation.

**Related** — [[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--lactate-and-oxygen-debt-myths]] (staging;
the direct source of the lactate-framing contest above — recommend the Verkhoshansky entry
add a reciprocal link back to this one once both are reviewed).

# Which Training Modalities Tolerate Fatigue, and Which Need a Fresh Athlete

**What it is** — Figure 2.3 (PDF p. 72, printed p. 60) ranks eleven training modalities by
how much athlete fatigue they can tolerate before the acute training effect is compromised,
from "well rested" through "slightly fatigued," "moderately fatigued," to "fatigued":
**require well-rested or only slightly fatigued athletes** — maximal speed (least
fatigue-tolerant of all), acquisition of new technical skills, explosive strength, maximal
strength (neural mechanism, e.g. 1-3RM); **tolerate up to moderate fatigue** — anaerobic
glycolytic power, technique perfection, aerobic power, maximal strength (hypertrophy, e.g.
8-10RM); **tolerate fatigue through to the end of the session (most fatigue-tolerant)** —
anaerobic glycolytic capacity/endurance, aerobic endurance (long duration), strength
endurance, flexibility. Issurin's stated reasoning (PDF pp. 71-73, printed pp. 60-62):
exercises needing precise excitatory neural output (max speed, explosive strength, technical
skill acquisition, neural-mechanism strength) are blocked by inhibitory CNS output in
fatigued athletes, so they belong early; anaerobic glycolytic power needs available energy
reserves that are depleted in fatigued athletes; hypertrophy-strength work depends on total
mechanical work and post-exercise recovery conditions (not the athlete's pre-exercise
freshness), so it can be placed later or even after an endurance session; anaerobic
glycolytic capacity and strength/aerobic endurance work are defined by sustained effort
*despite* accumulating fatigue, so some fatigue is expected and even required for the
intended stimulus.

**Why it works** — CNS-dependent, high-precision, high-velocity qualities are limited by
inhibitory neural output and available energy stores that both degrade with fatigue,
while volume/duration-dependent qualities (hypertrophy, strength/aerobic endurance) depend
on total accumulated work or post-session recovery rather than the athlete's moment-to-moment
freshness — so sequencing exists to protect the fatigue-sensitive qualities' window, not
because "harder exercises always go first."

**When to apply** — Ordering exercises within a single practice or lift: place max-speed
work, new skill acquisition, explosive strength, and low-rep neural-strength work at the
start of a session (or after only light warm-up fatigue); place hypertrophy work, technical
perfection under fatigue, and long-duration aerobic/strength-endurance work later, when some
accumulated fatigue is acceptable or even intended. Issurin gives a worked example (PDF
p. 72, printed p. 61): an endurance athlete needing to preserve muscle mass can have a
hypertrophy-focused strength session (8-10RM) placed *after* a medium-load endurance
session, because hypertrophy's driver is total mechanical work and post-workout recovery
conditions, not pre-workout freshness — this would be the wrong sequencing choice for a
neural-strength (1-3RM) session, which does need "prime time."

**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — **The author gives no primary citation for Figure 2.3
itself** — it reads as the author's own synthesized ranking rather than a reproduced,
independently-sourced scale; treat the ordinal ranking (which modality is more or less
fatigue-tolerant than its neighbor) as a reasonable but unvalidated synthesis, not a measured
result. The figure gives no guidance on *how much* fatigue is "slight" vs. "moderate" in
objective terms (RPE, HR, or specific fatigue markers), so applying it requires a coach's own
judgment call about where an athlete currently sits on that continuum. It also does not
address multi-session days directly — see [[heuristic--two-a-day-workout-sequencing-by-dominant-ability]]
for cross-session sequencing.

**Example** — A football practice combining new install (technical skill acquisition) with
conditioning: install work belongs at the start of practice when players are fresh and can
attend to technical detail; conditioning work belongs at the end, where sustained effort
under fatigue is the intended stimulus rather than a limitation.

**Related** — [[framework--key-workout-and-key-exercise-concept]],
[[principle--training-modality-compatibility-in-a-workout]].

15	# Case Study: Bondarchuk's Developmental/Competitive/Restorative Blocks and the 1988 Hammer Throw Podium
16	
17	**What it is** — Issurin credits Anatoly Bondarchuk, hammer-throw coach, with one of the
18	precursor systems to Block Periodization (PDF p. 32, printed p. 21). Based on his own
19	athletic career (1972 Olympic hammer-throw champion) and doctoral research on throwers'
20	training programs (1988), Bondarchuk built a periodization chart using three types of
21	specialized mesocycle-blocks: **developmental** (workload gradually increases to maximum),
22	**competitive** (load stabilizes, athletes focus on competitive performance), and
23	**restorative** (active recovery, preparing for the next developmental block). Stated
24	durations: developmental and competitive blocks are "usually four weeks," restorative "can
25	be shortened to two weeks." Sequencing depends on the competition schedule and individual
26	athlete response. The claimed outcome: Bondarchuk coached the gold, silver, and bronze
27	medalists in hammer throw at the 1988 Olympics — "the entire Olympic podium occupied by
28	athletes of the same coach" (Bondarchuk, 1986 and 1988, as cited by Issurin).
29	
30	**Why it works — the author gives no mechanism beyond the general BPC rationale** —
31	Issurin does not describe Bondarchuk's own stated reasoning for why these particular block
32	lengths (4/4/2 weeks) or this particular three-way split (by competitive readiness rather
33	than by ability type) were chosen; the mechanism offered is the same general BPC logic
34	(concentrated, sequenced blocks beat simultaneous multi-ability training) applied
35	retroactively to Bondarchuk's design.
36	
37	**When to apply — untested, use as a historical precedent, not as evidence** — Useful for
38	explaining the lineage of block-periodization thinking (Bondarchuk predates and directly
39	inspired Issurin's own accumulation/transmutation/realization taxonomy, per PDF p. 32-33)
40	and as an alternative three-block naming scheme organized around competitive readiness
41	(developmental/competitive/restorative) rather than ability type
42	(accumulation/transmutation/realization) — worth distinguishing the two schemes explicitly
43	when citing "Bondarchuk's blocks" versus "Issurin's blocks."
44	
45	**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — This is a single coach's single-event outcome (n = 1
46	coaching program, one Olympic final) with no comparison group, no report of what other
47	finalists' training looked like, and total reliance on the coach's and Issurin's own
48	secondary account rather than an independent case audit. A three-medal sweep at one Olympics
49	is a striking result but cannot isolate the training design's contribution from athlete
50	talent, competitor variance on the day, or other coaching factors. Do not cite this as
51	evidence that a 4/4/2-week block cadence "works" for hammer throw or any other event; it
52	illustrates a design, not a validated dose-response finding. This is distinct from and
53	should not be merged with Issurin's own accumulation/transmutation/realization taxonomy — see
54	[[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]] for that separate, though
55	historically related, three-block system.
56	
57	**Example** — A coach citing "block periodization has a track record" should specify
58	which system (Bondarchuk's competitive-readiness blocks or Issurin's ability-type blocks) and
59	should not present the 1988 podium sweep as generalizable evidence beyond "one documented
60	historical instance this concept coincided with a strong outcome."
61	
62	**Related** — [[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]],
63	[[case-study--issurin-kaverin-canoe-kayak-block-periodization]] — a comparable single-coach
64	case from the same era; consider also cross-referencing
65	`fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer/framework--sprint-exercise-classes-bondarchuk-four-categories.md`
66	(vault) — the *same* coach (Bondarchuk), but a completely different, unrelated framework
67	of his (an exercise-classification taxonomy by movement similarity, not a mesocycle-timing
68	system). The two should never be conflated when either is cited.

83	# Two Studies Issurin Cites Against Simultaneous Development: Swimmer Interference and Kayaker Decay
84	
85	**What it is** — Issurin presents two data-backed examples as motivation for abandoning
86	simultaneous multi-ability training (traditional periodization) in favor of consecutive,
87	concentrated blocks.
88	
89	**(1) Swimmer concurrent-training interference (PDF pp. 21-22, printed pp. 10-11, Figure
90	1.3).** High-level male swimmers were studied over an 8-week early-season program combining
91	extensive swimming with resistive/power dry-land work aimed at swim-specific strength
92	(9-11 workouts/week; sample size not stated in this text). Measured: maximal force of
93	tethered swimming (Ftsw), dry-land explosive strength (Fexp), and dry-land strength
94	endurance (SE). Result: strength endurance improved markedly; swim-specific strength did not
95	improve; explosive strength *decreased* — despite about 30% of dry-land program time devoted
96	to maximal/explosive strength work. Issurin's mechanistic explanation: extensive endurance
97	work captures the metabolic (anabolic) energy needed for the hypertrophy and neural-drive
98	adaptations that explosive/maximal strength require, and the resulting chronic fatigue keeps
99	central and peripheral neural factors from the state needed for strength gains
100	(citing Klausen, 1990, for the neural-mechanism point).
101	
102	**(2) Kayaker decay under traditional periodization (PDF p. 25-26, printed pp. 14-15,
103	Figure 1.4 — the in-text citation reads "Fig.1.3," which appears to be a labeling error in
104	the source; the described variables match Figure 1.4's caption, not Figure 1.3's).** A group
105	of highly qualified kayakers were tracked across a full annual cycle built on the classical
106	model (Issurin et al., 1986). Measured: mean distance velocity (Vd), velocity at anaerobic
107	threshold (V-AT), peak paddle force (PF), stroke rate (SR), muscle mass (MM). Result: the
108	long general-preparatory period raised V-AT, muscle mass and peak force substantially; but
109	during the extended, highly specialized competitive period, extensive aerobic work and
110	maximum-strength work were reduced or dropped as "harmful for racing technique," and V-AT,
111	peak force, and muscle mass all *declined* by the competitive period. Distance velocity
112	still reached its season maximum, but only via increased stroke rate compensating for
113	reduced force — i.e., technique/rate covered for a real loss in the underlying strength and
114	aerobic qualities. Issurin's summary: "the timing pattern for developing different abilities
115	was far from optimal."
116	
117	**Why it works** — For the swimmer case, Issurin's own stated mechanism is that extensive
118	endurance work "captures the metabolic energy that is necessary for anabolism during
119	post-exercise recovery," suppressing the muscle hypertrophy and neural-drive adaptations
120	strength training requires, and that chronic fatigue from high-volume training keeps
121	"central and peripheral neural factors... far from optimum" (PDF pp. 21-22, printed pp.
122	10-11, citing Klausen, 1990, for the neural-mechanism point). For the kayaker case, Issurin
123	gives no physiological mechanism for the decline beyond narration of what happened (reduced
124	aerobic and strength work during the competitive period, PDF p. 25, printed p. 14) — treat
125	that case as a described pattern, not an explained one. **Inference:** labeling the two
126	cases as "concurrent interference" versus "sequential decay" is this entry's own
127	categorization for cross-referencing purposes, not language Issurin himself uses; both are
128	offered by Issurin as evidence for the same underlying argument against simultaneous,
129	non-block training (see [[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]]), which in turn
130	motivates the consecutive block sequencing in
131	[[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]] and
132	[[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]].
133	
134	**When to apply** — The swimmer study is the stronger evidence of the two: it is a
135	controlled, measured 8-week study with named outcome variables, giving concrete numbers
136	useful for illustrating concurrent-training interference to Baylor strength staff
137	programming for athletes who need both an aerobic base and explosive/max strength (e.g.,
138	many football positions in a fall-camp conditioning window). The kayaker case is useful
139	mainly as a cautionary illustration of "building a quality early in the year and then
140	letting it decay unaddressed."
141	
142	**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — The swimmer study's exact sample size is not given in
143	this text (only workout frequency, 9-11/week), so its statistical strength cannot be judged
144	from this source alone — treat the direction of the finding (interference occurred) as
145	`supported` but the specific numeric changes in Figure 1.3 as unverifiable without the
146	original 1986/whichever-year source Issurin drew Figure 1.3 from (not cited by name on this
147	page). **Untested:** the kayaker case is Issurin's own team's data (Issurin et al., 1986),
148	observational across one season with no control group — it demonstrates a plausible pattern,
149	not a controlled comparison against an alternative periodization model run on the same
150	athletes. Neither study is football-specific; football's in-season structure (weekly
151	competition, not one late-season peak) differs from both the swimmers' fixed 8-week block and
152	the kayakers' single annual peak design.
153	
154	**Example** — A Baylor position group with both an in-season conditioning demand and a
155	strength-maintenance demand should treat "just add more of both" as the swimmer study's
156	failure mode: without deliberate sequencing or volume management, the concurrent aerobic
157	load can blunt the intended strength/power adaptation even when strength work is
158	programmed.
159	
160	**Related** — [[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]] (Table 1.4's rationale,
161	which these two studies are offered as concrete illustrations of),
162	[[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]].

177	# Case Study: The USSR Canoe-Kayak Team and the Original Accumulation/Transmutation/Realization Design
178	
179	**What it is** — Issurin's own account of where his accumulation-transmutation-realization
180	taxonomy came from (PDF p. 33, printed p. 22): in the early 1980s, elite USSR canoe-kayak
181	paddlers were training an "enormous exercise volume" that the author and colleagues judged
182	excessive. The block-and-mesocycle-sequencing idea was "conceptualized, implemented and
183	proved in practice" with the national team, then published (Issurin & Kaverin, 1985). The
184	modified design allowed "about a 10-15% reduction in the annual training volume." Follow-up
185	testing during preparation reportedly showed "considerable improvement in the main fitness
186	components in all subgroups." The claimed competitive outcomes: three gold and three silver
187	medals at the 1988 Seoul Olympics, and eight gold medals (1989) and nine gold medals (1990)
188	at the World Championships.
189	
190	**Why it works — the author's own interpretation, not independently verified here** —
191	Issurin attributes the improvement to reduced simultaneous multi-ability training and better
192	volume management under the new block structure, consistent with the general BPC rationale
193	in [[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]]. No comparison data (e.g., what the
194	same team's results looked like in prior Olympic/World Championship cycles under the old
195	model, or what other nations' medal counts did over the same period) is presented in this
196	chapter to isolate the training-design change from other factors (athlete development,
197	equipment, competitor turnover).
198	
199	**When to apply — untested, treat as the concept's origin story, not as proof** — Useful
200	as the direct provenance of Issurin's own taxonomy (see
201	[[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]]) and as a data point that a
202	national federation with centralized, well-resourced athlete monitoring implemented this
203	design at scale (not just with one athlete).
204	
205	**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — This is the concept's inventor reporting on his own
206	uncontrolled intervention with his own national team, published by the same author (Issurin
207	& Kaverin, 1985) — the account here (2008 book) is a secondary retelling with no cited
208	independent replication or outcome audit. As with the Bondarchuk case, do not treat the
209	Olympic and World Championship medal counts as a controlled test of the training design;
210	1980s Soviet sport had structural advantages (centralized athlete development, resourcing)
211	that are not present in most other training contexts, including a US college football
212	program. The "10-15% volume reduction" figure has no comparison baseline stated (reduction
213	from what specific prior volume, over what specific prior period) beyond "the annual
214	training volume."
215	
216	**Example** — Citing "block periodization produced Olympic medals" should specify this is
217	one 1980s Soviet national-team case reported by the method's own originator, not a
218	controlled trial, and should be paired with the caveat already logged in
219	[[case-study--bondarchuk-hammer-throw-block-mesocycles]] about single-coach, single-program
220	evidence.
221	
222	**Related** — [[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]],
223	[[case-study--bondarchuk-hammer-throw-block-mesocycles]].

238	# Squat-First vs. Squat-After-Hang-Pull Changes Whether You Get More Reps or More Power
239	
240	**What it is** — Spreuwenberg et al. (2006), cited by Issurin (PDF p. 73, printed p. 62):
241	**nine** resistance-trained male athletes performed the back squat (4 sets at 85% of 1RM) on
242	two separate days under two protocols. Protocol A: squat performed during the initial part
243	of the workout. Protocol B: squat performed after a whole-body resistance exercise (hang
244	pull). Results: Protocol A produced significantly more repetitions per set (8.0 ± 1.9 vs.
245	5.4 ± 2.7 in Protocol B), but average power per set was *higher* in Protocol B. Issurin
246	attributes the power difference to postactivation potentiation induced by the preceding
247	whole-body power exercise.
248	
249	**Why it works** — Issurin reports only the study authors' own attribution for the power
250	finding: they "attributed this phenomenon to postactivation potentiation induced by the
251	preceding whole-body power exercise" (PDF p. 73, printed p. 62). **Inference:** the
252	companion explanation for the rep-count finding, that fresh (unfatigued) muscle sustains
253	more total repetitions at a given relative load than muscle that has just performed a
254	preceding whole-body lift, is this entry's own reasoning to account for the Protocol A
255	result; Issurin does not state that explanation for the rep-count difference in this
256	passage.
257	
258	**When to apply** — Choosing exercise order based on the specific training goal for that
259	session: Issurin's stated takeaway (PDF p. 73, printed p. 62) is that a coach wanting maximum
260	hypertrophy stimulus should place the squat early in the session (more total volume/reps),
261	while a coach targeting maximum power output should place it after appropriate whole-body
262	resistance work, to exploit postactivation potentiation. Directly usable for Baylor
263	strength-staff session design when max-effort lower-body power output (not volume) is the
264	stated goal of a given lift.
265	
266	**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — This is a small (n = 9), single published study;
267	Issurin does not report effect sizes, statistical significance values, or the specific
268	whole-body exercise's loading in this citation beyond "hang pull" — treat the direction of
269	the finding as `supported` but do not treat the exact magnitude (8.0 vs. 5.4 reps) as
270	something to replicate precisely without reading the original study. It is unclear from this
271	text whether the postactivation-potentiation effect generalizes to different athlete
272	populations (this sample was resistance-trained males), different preceding exercises, or
273	different rest intervals between the potentiating exercise and the squat.
274	
275	**Example** — A power-focused lower-body day for football linemen might sequence a
276	moderate-load hang pull or clean pull before back squats at 85% 1RM, accepting fewer total
277	squat reps in exchange for higher power output per rep on the squats that follow — a
278	hypertrophy-focused day for the same lift would instead put the squat first.
279	
280	**Related** — [[heuristic--exercise-sequencing-by-fatigue-state]],
281	[[principle--training-modality-compatibility-in-a-workout]].

295	
296	# A Structured Warm-Up/Cool-Down Program Cut Soccer Injuries Roughly Four-Fold Over Six Months
297	
298	**What it is** — Ekstrand et al. (1983), cited by Issurin (PDF p. 58, printed p. 47,
299	Figure 2.1): **twelve** national-division soccer teams (**180 players**) were split into two
300	groups. The intervention group (six teams) used a modified program with carefully structured
301	warm-ups (ball exercises plus a stretching program) and cool-downs (jogging plus hold-relax
302	stretching), supervised by doctors and physiotherapists. The control group (six teams)
303	trained traditionally. Over a six-month follow-up, the intervention group showed "highly
304	significant superiority": a roughly **four-fold reduction in the number of injuries** and a
305	"drastic decrease" in workouts and games missed to musculoskeletal disorders. Issurin
306	separately cites supporting single-factor findings: stretching in warm-up increases lower
307	extremity range of motion in soccer players (Moller et al., 1985); active warm-up *without*
308	stretching does not affect flexibility (Zakas et al., 2006); and intense prior exercise
309	meaningfully stimulates aerobic metabolism in working muscles during subsequent strenuous
310	performance (Bangsbo et al., 2001). A related study (Moller et al., 1985, PDF p. 68, printed
311	p. 57) tracked 48 adult soccer players across three warm-up/cool-down protocols and found
312	that inserting a stretching series into the *cool-down* (not just the warm-up) produced range-
313	of-motion benefits both immediately after the session and 24 hours later, while stretching
314	only in the warm-up helped immediately but not at 24 hours.
315	
316	**Why it works** — Issurin frames warm-up and cool-down as serving three functions each:
317	metabolic adjustment, technical/coordination adjustment, and mental readiness (warm-up,
318	Table 2.6, PDF p. 60, printed p. 49); and reduction of body temperature/HR/blood pressure,
319	removal of metabolic byproducts, endocrine-system recovery, and reduced emotional tension
320	(cool-down, Table 2.11, PDF p. 69, printed p. 58). **Contested — flag directly:** Issurin's
321	cool-down rationale explicitly frames blood lactate and "other acid metabolites" as "waste
322	products" to be "removed" from the muscles (PDF p. 68-69, printed pp. 57-58), citing a
323	specific clearance kinetic (blood lactate removal after a 4-minute exhausting time trial
324	takes about 20 minutes, Juel et al., 1990). This is in tension with a modern-physiology
325	claim already captured in this library's Verkhoshansky staging
326	([[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--lactate-and-oxygen-debt-myths]], `proven`): lactate is
327	not a toxin causing soreness or requiring active "removal," and it clears from the blood on
328	its own within about an hour of strenuous exercise regardless of cool-down activity, with
329	current research attributing post-exercise soreness to muscle/connective-tissue microtrauma
330	rather than residual lactate. The specific clearance-time citation (20 minutes for a 4-minute
331	time trial) may still be a real kinetic fact — that is not itself disputed here — but
332	Issurin's *framing* of this as evidence that cool-down actively "removes" a harmful waste
333	product reflects the outdated "lactic acid as toxin" model the Verkhoshansky entry corrects.
334	Cite this book's clearance-time number without repeating its waste-product framing.
335	
336	**When to apply** — The Ekstrand et al. (1983) result is directly relevant to Applied
337	Performance's collaboration with Athletic Medicine on injury reduction: a structured,
338	medically-supervised warm-up/cool-down protocol is associated with a large, measured
339	reduction in soft-tissue injury incidence in a team sport, over a real six-month season, not
340	an acute lab measure. The cool-down-stretching timing finding (Moller et al., 1985) suggests
341	cool-down, not just warm-up, is where a stretching series may do more for next-day range of
342	motion.
343	
344	**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — This is an observational, non-randomized team-level
345	comparison (teams chose or were assigned to conditions; individual randomization is not
346	described), and the intervention bundled multiple changes at once (warm-up content, cool-down
347	content, and medical/physiotherapy supervision), so the four-fold injury reduction cannot be
348	attributed to warm-up or cool-down alone — Issurin himself flags this study as "atypical
349	because it refers to the complex effects of warming-up, cooling-down and medical supervision"
350	(PDF p. 58, printed p. 47). **Contested:** stretching's effect on preventing delayed-onset
351	muscle soreness specifically is described by Issurin himself as disputed within this same
352	chapter — "supported by several studies (Hartfield, 1985) and contradicted by others (High
353	et al., 1989)" (PDF p. 70, printed p. 59) — do not cite stretching-prevents-DOMS as settled.
354	
355	**Example** — A Baylor position group's practice-ending routine that pairs light locomotion
356	with a stretching series (rather than stretching only in the pre-practice warm-up) has some
357	support here for next-day range-of-motion benefit, though the causal strength of the
358	underlying Moller et al. (1985) study for injury outcomes specifically (as opposed to ROM)
359	is not established by this citation.
360	
361	**Related** — [[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--lactate-and-oxygen-debt-myths]] (staging;
362	the direct source of the lactate-framing contest above — recommend the Verkhoshansky entry
363	add a reciprocal link back to this one once both are reviewed).

378	# Which Training Modalities Tolerate Fatigue, and Which Need a Fresh Athlete
379	
380	**What it is** — Figure 2.3 (PDF p. 72, printed p. 60) ranks eleven training modalities by
381	how much athlete fatigue they can tolerate before the acute training effect is compromised,
382	from "well rested" through "slightly fatigued," "moderately fatigued," to "fatigued":
383	**require well-rested or only slightly fatigued athletes** — maximal speed (least
384	fatigue-tolerant of all), acquisition of new technical skills, explosive strength, maximal
385	strength (neural mechanism, e.g. 1-3RM); **tolerate up to moderate fatigue** — anaerobic
386	glycolytic power, technique perfection, aerobic power, maximal strength (hypertrophy, e.g.
387	8-10RM); **tolerate fatigue through to the end of the session (most fatigue-tolerant)** —
388	anaerobic glycolytic capacity/endurance, aerobic endurance (long duration), strength
389	endurance, flexibility. Issurin's stated reasoning (PDF pp. 71-73, printed pp. 60-62):
390	exercises needing precise excitatory neural output (max speed, explosive strength, technical
391	skill acquisition, neural-mechanism strength) are blocked by inhibitory CNS output in
392	fatigued athletes, so they belong early; anaerobic glycolytic power needs available energy
393	reserves that are depleted in fatigued athletes; hypertrophy-strength work depends on total
394	mechanical work and post-exercise recovery conditions (not the athlete's pre-exercise
395	freshness), so it can be placed later or even after an endurance session; anaerobic
396	glycolytic capacity and strength/aerobic endurance work are defined by sustained effort
397	*despite* accumulating fatigue, so some fatigue is expected and even required for the
398	intended stimulus.
399	
400	**Why it works** — CNS-dependent, high-precision, high-velocity qualities are limited by
401	inhibitory neural output and available energy stores that both degrade with fatigue,
402	while volume/duration-dependent qualities (hypertrophy, strength/aerobic endurance) depend
403	on total accumulated work or post-session recovery rather than the athlete's moment-to-moment
404	freshness — so sequencing exists to protect the fatigue-sensitive qualities' window, not
405	because "harder exercises always go first."
406	
407	**When to apply** — Ordering exercises within a single practice or lift: place max-speed
408	work, new skill acquisition, explosive strength, and low-rep neural-strength work at the
409	start of a session (or after only light warm-up fatigue); place hypertrophy work, technical
410	perfection under fatigue, and long-duration aerobic/strength-endurance work later, when some
411	accumulated fatigue is acceptable or even intended. Issurin gives a worked example (PDF
412	p. 72, printed p. 61): an endurance athlete needing to preserve muscle mass can have a
413	hypertrophy-focused strength session (8-10RM) placed *after* a medium-load endurance
414	session, because hypertrophy's driver is total mechanical work and post-workout recovery
415	conditions, not pre-workout freshness — this would be the wrong sequencing choice for a
416	neural-strength (1-3RM) session, which does need "prime time."
417	
418	**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — **The author gives no primary citation for Figure 2.3
419	itself** — it reads as the author's own synthesized ranking rather than a reproduced,
420	independently-sourced scale; treat the ordinal ranking (which modality is more or less
421	fatigue-tolerant than its neighbor) as a reasonable but unvalidated synthesis, not a measured
422	result. The figure gives no guidance on *how much* fatigue is "slight" vs. "moderate" in
423	objective terms (RPE, HR, or specific fatigue markers), so applying it requires a coach's own
424	judgment call about where an athlete currently sits on that continuum. It also does not
425	address multi-session days directly — see [[heuristic--two-a-day-workout-sequencing-by-dominant-ability]]
426	for cross-session sequencing.
427	
428	**Example** — A football practice combining new install (technical skill acquisition) with
429	conditioning: install work belongs at the start of practice when players are fresh and can
430	attend to technical detail; conditioning work belongs at the end, where sustained effort
431	under fatigue is the intended stimulus rather than a limitation.
432	
433	**Related** — [[framework--key-workout-and-key-exercise-concept]],
434	[[principle--training-modality-compatibility-in-a-workout]].
435	######## heuristic--two-a-day-workout-sequencing-by-dominant-ability.md
436	---
437	type: library-entry
438	kind: heuristic
439	domain: strength-and-conditioning
440	book: block-periodization--issurin
441	chapter: "2.3.3"
442	topic: sequencing multiple same-day training sessions
443	category: [scheduling, multi-session, programming]
444	confidence: supported
445	ingest-tier: full-text
446	created: 2026-09-26
447	---
448	
449	# Structuring Two-a-Day (and Denser) Training Days by Dominant Ability and Rest Interval
450	
451	**What it is** — Issurin describes how high-performance programs structure multiple same-day
452	sessions, most commonly two-a-days but up to four (routine in training-camp practice) or
453	occasionally six (an "exception," per anecdotal coach reports, PDF p. 76, printed p. 65). For
454	a four-session aerobic-development day (Figure 2.5, PDF p. 77, printed p. 66): session 1
455	(early morning) uses small load — warm-up, alactic bouts combined with medium-intensity
456	aerobic work, addressing morning stiffness/soreness; session 2 (mid-morning, after a
457	multi-hour break) uses medium/substantial load — aerobic interval series combined with
458	technical tasks, where sprint bouts interact positively with the aerobic work; session 3
459	(early afternoon, after a one-hour break) uses medium/substantial load — concentrated aerobic
460	work; session 4 (late afternoon, after a three-hour break) uses substantial load — continuous
461	aerobic exercise and aerobic-resistance work, with an emphasized, longer cool-down given
462	accumulated fatigue. For anaerobic-development days (Figure 2.6, PDF p. 78, printed p. 67):
463	session 2 uses substantial load for anaerobic glycolytic power (fast lactate/oxygen-debt
464	accumulation); the one-hour break before session 3 allows roughly 70-80% of accumulated
465	lactate to be oxidized (Volkov, 1986), so session 3's anaerobic glycolytic capacity work
466	still starts with an already-activated glycolytic/enzymatic system; session 4 (after a
467	three-hour break, athletes arriving fatigued) targets anaerobic strength endurance,
468	deliberately sustaining progressive fatigue. For the more common two-a-day structure, Table
469	2.13 (PDF p. 79, printed p. 68) gives compatible first/second-workout pairings by dominant
470	ability: aerobic power/capacity — fartlek (10-15s sprint, 3-6min at anaerobic threshold)
471	first, aerobic interval series second; anaerobic glycolytic power/capacity — anaerobic power
472	interval series first, anaerobic capacity interval series second; maximal speed — anaerobic
473	alactic interval series first, anaerobic alactic plus explosive strength exercises second;
474	techno-tactical abilities — techno-tactical simulation/maximum speed first, match/scrimmage
475	second.
476	
477	**Why it works** — The break length between sessions determines how much of the prior
478	session's fatigue and metabolic byproduct load has cleared before the next session begins,
479	and the daily plan deliberately exploits this: shorter breaks (one hour) leave residual
480	glycolytic activation that *helps* a subsequent glycolytic-capacity session, while longer
481	breaks (three hours) still leave athletes fatigued enough that only fatigue-tolerant
482	modalities (strength endurance, continuous aerobic work) are appropriate for the day's final
483	session.
484	
485	**When to apply** — Directly applicable to football fall-camp scheduling, where two-a-day
486	sessions are standard. **Eric's baseline** names a specific priority stack for fall camp —
487	"Goal 1, alactic and aerobic capacity/power for fall-camp demands" (`method-baseline.md`,
488	"Conditioning and energy systems," citing `class-4-2026.md` pp.34, 39) — and Table 2.13's
489	maximal-speed pairing (anaerobic alactic interval series both sessions, explosive strength
490	added to the second) is a directly relevant template for structuring a two-a-day built
491	around that same alactic/aerobic priority.
492	
493	**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — Issurin gives no controlled-study citation for the
494	specific figures in this section (session load levels, the four-session structure, the
495	70-80% lactate-oxidation-in-one-hour figure attributed to Volkov, 1986, is the one sourced
496	number; the rest of the daily-series structure reads as the author's own applied synthesis).
497	The four-session model is explicitly noted as less common in practice than the two-a-day.
498	**Inference:** none of this section's examples are football-specific (they are framed around
499	individual/endurance-and-power sports generally); the specific break lengths (one hour,
500	three hours) and load progressions should be treated as a template to adapt, not a
501	prescription to copy directly into a football fall-camp schedule without accounting for
502	football-specific factors (equipment, heat, practice structure, position-group differences)
503	not addressed in this chapter.
504	
505	**Example** — A fall-camp two-a-day built around the department's stated alactic/aerobic
506	priority could pair a morning session of alactic interval sprint work with an afternoon
507	session combining more alactic work and explosive strength (per Table 2.13's maximal-speed
508	row), rather than defaulting to a generic "conditioning AM, lift PM" split that does not
509	target a specific dominant ability across the two sessions.
510	
511	**Related** — [[claim--morning-resistance-training-no-decrement-after-6hr-rest]],
512	[[heuristic--exercise-sequencing-by-fatigue-state]],
513	[[principle--training-modality-compatibility-in-a-workout]].

# Case Study: Bondarchuk's Developmental/Competitive/Restorative Blocks and the 1988 Hammer Throw Podium

**What it is** — Issurin credits Anatoly Bondarchuk, hammer-throw coach, with one of the
precursor systems to Block Periodization (PDF p. 32, printed p. 21). Based on his own
athletic career (1972 Olympic hammer-throw champion) and doctoral research on throwers'
training programs (1988), Bondarchuk built a periodization chart using three types of
specialized mesocycle-blocks: **developmental** (workload gradually increases to maximum),
**competitive** (load stabilizes, athletes focus on competitive performance), and
**restorative** (active recovery, preparing for the next developmental block). Stated
durations: developmental and competitive blocks are "usually four weeks," restorative "can
be shortened to two weeks." Sequencing depends on the competition schedule and individual
athlete response. The claimed outcome: Bondarchuk coached the gold, silver, and bronze
medalists in hammer throw at the 1988 Olympics — "the entire Olympic podium occupied by
athletes of the same coach" (Bondarchuk, 1986 and 1988, as cited by Issurin).

**Why it works — the author gives no mechanism beyond the general BPC rationale** —
Issurin does not describe Bondarchuk's own stated reasoning for why these particular block
lengths (4/4/2 weeks) or this particular three-way split (by competitive readiness rather
than by ability type) were chosen; the mechanism offered is the same general BPC logic
(concentrated, sequenced blocks beat simultaneous multi-ability training) applied
retroactively to Bondarchuk's design.

**When to apply — untested, use as a historical precedent, not as evidence** — Useful for
explaining the lineage of block-periodization thinking (Bondarchuk predates and directly
inspired Issurin's own accumulation/transmutation/realization taxonomy, per PDF p. 32-33)
and as an alternative three-block naming scheme organized around competitive readiness
(developmental/competitive/restorative) rather than ability type
(accumulation/transmutation/realization) — worth distinguishing the two schemes explicitly
when citing "Bondarchuk's blocks" versus "Issurin's blocks."

**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — This is a single coach's single-event outcome (n = 1
coaching program, one Olympic final) with no comparison group, no report of what other
finalists' training looked like, and total reliance on the coach's and Issurin's own
secondary account rather than an independent case audit. A three-medal sweep at one Olympics
is a striking result but cannot isolate the training design's contribution from athlete
talent, competitor variance on the day, or other coaching factors. Do not cite this as
evidence that a 4/4/2-week block cadence "works" for hammer throw or any other event; it
illustrates a design, not a validated dose-response finding. This is distinct from and
should not be merged with Issurin's own accumulation/transmutation/realization taxonomy — see
[[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]] for that separate, though
historically related, three-block system.

**Example** — A coach citing "block periodization has a track record" should specify
which system (Bondarchuk's competitive-readiness blocks or Issurin's ability-type blocks) and
should not present the 1988 podium sweep as generalizable evidence beyond "one documented
historical instance this concept coincided with a strong outcome."

**Related** — [[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]],
[[case-study--issurin-kaverin-canoe-kayak-block-periodization]] — a comparable single-coach
case from the same era; consider also cross-referencing
`fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer/framework--sprint-exercise-classes-bondarchuk-four-categories.md`
(vault) — the *same* coach (Bondarchuk), but a completely different, unrelated framework
of his (an exercise-classification taxonomy by movement similarity, not a mesocycle-timing
system). The two should never be conflated when either is cited.

# Two Studies Issurin Cites Against Simultaneous Development: Swimmer Interference and Kayaker Decay

**What it is** — Issurin presents two data-backed examples as motivation for abandoning
simultaneous multi-ability training (traditional periodization) in favor of consecutive,
concentrated blocks.

**(1) Swimmer concurrent-training interference (PDF pp. 21-22, printed pp. 10-11, Figure
1.3).** High-level male swimmers were studied over an 8-week early-season program combining
extensive swimming with resistive/power dry-land work aimed at swim-specific strength
(9-11 workouts/week; sample size not stated in this text). Measured: maximal force of
tethered swimming (Ftsw), dry-land explosive strength (Fexp), and dry-land strength
endurance (SE). Result: strength endurance improved markedly; swim-specific strength did not
improve; explosive strength *decreased* — despite about 30% of dry-land program time devoted
to maximal/explosive strength work. Issurin's mechanistic explanation: extensive endurance
work captures the metabolic (anabolic) energy needed for the hypertrophy and neural-drive
adaptations that explosive/maximal strength require, and the resulting chronic fatigue keeps
central and peripheral neural factors from the state needed for strength gains
(citing Klausen, 1990, for the neural-mechanism point).

**(2) Kayaker decay under traditional periodization (PDF p. 25-26, printed pp. 14-15,
Figure 1.4 — the in-text citation reads "Fig.1.3," which appears to be a labeling error in
the source; the described variables match Figure 1.4's caption, not Figure 1.3's).** A group
of highly qualified kayakers were tracked across a full annual cycle built on the classical
model (Issurin et al., 1986). Measured: mean distance velocity (Vd), velocity at anaerobic
threshold (V-AT), peak paddle force (PF), stroke rate (SR), muscle mass (MM). Result: the
long general-preparatory period raised V-AT, muscle mass and peak force substantially; but
during the extended, highly specialized competitive period, extensive aerobic work and
maximum-strength work were reduced or dropped as "harmful for racing technique," and V-AT,
peak force, and muscle mass all *declined* by the competitive period. Distance velocity
still reached its season maximum, but only via increased stroke rate compensating for
reduced force — i.e., technique/rate covered for a real loss in the underlying strength and
aerobic qualities. Issurin's summary: "the timing pattern for developing different abilities
was far from optimal."

**Why it works** — For the swimmer case, Issurin's own stated mechanism is that extensive
endurance work "captures the metabolic energy that is necessary for anabolism during
post-exercise recovery," suppressing the muscle hypertrophy and neural-drive adaptations
strength training requires, and that chronic fatigue from high-volume training keeps
"central and peripheral neural factors... far from optimum" (PDF pp. 21-22, printed pp.
10-11, citing Klausen, 1990, for the neural-mechanism point). For the kayaker case, Issurin
gives no physiological mechanism for the decline beyond narration of what happened (reduced
aerobic and strength work during the competitive period, PDF p. 25, printed p. 14) — treat
that case as a described pattern, not an explained one. **Inference:** labeling the two
cases as "concurrent interference" versus "sequential decay" is this entry's own
categorization for cross-referencing purposes, not language Issurin himself uses; both are
offered by Issurin as evidence for the same underlying argument against simultaneous,
non-block training (see [[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]]), which in turn
motivates the consecutive block sequencing in
[[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]] and
[[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]].

**When to apply** — The swimmer study is the stronger evidence of the two: it is a
controlled, measured 8-week study with named outcome variables, giving concrete numbers
useful for illustrating concurrent-training interference to Baylor strength staff
programming for athletes who need both an aerobic base and explosive/max strength (e.g.,
many football positions in a fall-camp conditioning window). The kayaker case is useful
mainly as a cautionary illustration of "building a quality early in the year and then
letting it decay unaddressed."

**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — The swimmer study's exact sample size is not given in
this text (only workout frequency, 9-11/week), so its statistical strength cannot be judged
from this source alone — treat the direction of the finding (interference occurred) as
`supported` but the specific numeric changes in Figure 1.3 as unverifiable without the
original 1986/whichever-year source Issurin drew Figure 1.3 from (not cited by name on this
page). **Untested:** the kayaker case is Issurin's own team's data (Issurin et al., 1986),
observational across one season with no control group — it demonstrates a plausible pattern,
not a controlled comparison against an alternative periodization model run on the same
athletes. Neither study is football-specific; football's in-season structure (weekly
competition, not one late-season peak) differs from both the swimmers' fixed 8-week block and
the kayakers' single annual peak design.

**Example** — A Baylor position group with both an in-season conditioning demand and a
strength-maintenance demand should treat "just add more of both" as the swimmer study's
failure mode: without deliberate sequencing or volume management, the concurrent aerobic
load can blunt the intended strength/power adaptation even when strength work is
programmed.

**Related** — [[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]] (Table 1.4's rationale,
which these two studies are offered as concrete illustrations of),
[[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]].

# Case Study: The USSR Canoe-Kayak Team and the Original Accumulation/Transmutation/Realization Design

**What it is** — Issurin's own account of where his accumulation-transmutation-realization
taxonomy came from (PDF p. 33, printed p. 22): in the early 1980s, elite USSR canoe-kayak
paddlers were training an "enormous exercise volume" that the author and colleagues judged
excessive. The block-and-mesocycle-sequencing idea was "conceptualized, implemented and
proved in practice" with the national team, then published (Issurin & Kaverin, 1985). The
modified design allowed "about a 10-15% reduction in the annual training volume." Follow-up
testing during preparation reportedly showed "considerable improvement in the main fitness
components in all subgroups." The claimed competitive outcomes: three gold and three silver
medals at the 1988 Seoul Olympics, and eight gold medals (1989) and nine gold medals (1990)
at the World Championships.

**Why it works — the author's own interpretation, not independently verified here** —
Issurin attributes the improvement to reduced simultaneous multi-ability training and better
volume management under the new block structure, consistent with the general BPC rationale
in [[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]]. No comparison data (e.g., what the
same team's results looked like in prior Olympic/World Championship cycles under the old
model, or what other nations' medal counts did over the same period) is presented in this
chapter to isolate the training-design change from other factors (athlete development,
equipment, competitor turnover).

**When to apply — untested, treat as the concept's origin story, not as proof** — Useful
as the direct provenance of Issurin's own taxonomy (see
[[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]]) and as a data point that a
national federation with centralized, well-resourced athlete monitoring implemented this
design at scale (not just with one athlete).

**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — This is the concept's inventor reporting on his own
uncontrolled intervention with his own national team, published by the same author (Issurin
& Kaverin, 1985) — the account here (2008 book) is a secondary retelling with no cited
independent replication or outcome audit. As with the Bondarchuk case, do not treat the
Olympic and World Championship medal counts as a controlled test of the training design;
1980s Soviet sport had structural advantages (centralized athlete development, resourcing)
that are not present in most other training contexts, including a US college football
program. The "10-15% volume reduction" figure has no comparison baseline stated (reduction
from what specific prior volume, over what specific prior period) beyond "the annual
training volume."

**Example** — Citing "block periodization produced Olympic medals" should specify this is
one 1980s Soviet national-team case reported by the method's own originator, not a
controlled trial, and should be paired with the caveat already logged in
[[case-study--bondarchuk-hammer-throw-block-mesocycles]] about single-coach, single-program
evidence.

**Related** — [[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]],
[[case-study--bondarchuk-hammer-throw-block-mesocycles]].

# Squat-First vs. Squat-After-Hang-Pull Changes Whether You Get More Reps or More Power

**What it is** — Spreuwenberg et al. (2006), cited by Issurin (PDF p. 73, printed p. 62):
**nine** resistance-trained male athletes performed the back squat (4 sets at 85% of 1RM) on
two separate days under two protocols. Protocol A: squat performed during the initial part
of the workout. Protocol B: squat performed after a whole-body resistance exercise (hang
pull). Results: Protocol A produced significantly more repetitions per set (8.0 ± 1.9 vs.
5.4 ± 2.7 in Protocol B), but average power per set was *higher* in Protocol B. Issurin
attributes the power difference to postactivation potentiation induced by the preceding
whole-body power exercise.

**Why it works** — Issurin reports only the study authors' own attribution for the power
finding: they "attributed this phenomenon to postactivation potentiation induced by the
preceding whole-body power exercise" (PDF p. 73, printed p. 62). **Inference:** the
companion explanation for the rep-count finding, that fresh (unfatigued) muscle sustains
more total repetitions at a given relative load than muscle that has just performed a
preceding whole-body lift, is this entry's own reasoning to account for the Protocol A
result; Issurin does not state that explanation for the rep-count difference in this
passage.

**When to apply** — Choosing exercise order based on the specific training goal for that
session: Issurin's stated takeaway (PDF p. 73, printed p. 62) is that a coach wanting maximum
hypertrophy stimulus should place the squat early in the session (more total volume/reps),
while a coach targeting maximum power output should place it after appropriate whole-body
resistance work, to exploit postactivation potentiation. Directly usable for Baylor
strength-staff session design when max-effort lower-body power output (not volume) is the
stated goal of a given lift.

**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — This is a small (n = 9), single published study;
Issurin does not report effect sizes, statistical significance values, or the specific
whole-body exercise's loading in this citation beyond "hang pull" — treat the direction of
the finding as `supported` but do not treat the exact magnitude (8.0 vs. 5.4 reps) as
something to replicate precisely without reading the original study. It is unclear from this
text whether the postactivation-potentiation effect generalizes to different athlete
populations (this sample was resistance-trained males), different preceding exercises, or
different rest intervals between the potentiating exercise and the squat.

**Example** — A power-focused lower-body day for football linemen might sequence a
moderate-load hang pull or clean pull before back squats at 85% 1RM, accepting fewer total
squat reps in exchange for higher power output per rep on the squats that follow — a
hypertrophy-focused day for the same lift would instead put the squat first.

**Related** — [[heuristic--exercise-sequencing-by-fatigue-state]],
[[principle--training-modality-compatibility-in-a-workout]].
######## case-study--warmup-cooldown-injury-reduction-soccer.md
---
type: library-entry
kind: case-study
domain: strength-and-conditioning
book: block-periodization--issurin
chapter: "2.2.1, 2.2.3"
topic: warm-up/cool-down protocol and injury reduction
category: [injury-prevention, warm-up, case-study]
confidence: supported
ingest-tier: full-text
