---

# A Structured Warm-Up/Cool-Down Program Cut Soccer Injuries Roughly Four-Fold Over Six Months

**What it is** — Ekstrand et al. (1983), cited by Issurin (PDF p. 58, printed p. 47,
Figure 2.1): **twelve** national-division soccer teams (**180 players**) were split into two
groups. The intervention group (six teams) used a modified program with carefully structured
warm-ups (ball exercises plus a stretching program) and cool-downs (jogging plus hold-relax
stretching), supervised by doctors and physiotherapists. The control group (six teams)
trained traditionally. Over a six-month follow-up, the intervention group showed "highly
significant superiority": a roughly **four-fold reduction in the number of injuries** and a
"drastic decrease" in workouts and games missed to musculoskeletal disorders. Issurin
separately cites supporting single-factor findings: stretching in warm-up increases lower
extremity range of motion in soccer players (Moller et al., 1985); active warm-up *without*
stretching does not affect flexibility (Zakas et al., 2006); and intense prior exercise
meaningfully stimulates aerobic metabolism in working muscles during subsequent strenuous
performance (Bangsbo et al., 2001). A related study (Moller et al., 1985, PDF p. 68, printed
p. 57) tracked 48 adult soccer players across three warm-up/cool-down protocols and found
that inserting a stretching series into the *cool-down* (not just the warm-up) produced range-
of-motion benefits both immediately after the session and 24 hours later, while stretching
only in the warm-up helped immediately but not at 24 hours.

**Why it works** — Issurin frames warm-up and cool-down as serving three functions each:
metabolic adjustment, technical/coordination adjustment, and mental readiness (warm-up,
Table 2.6, PDF p. 60, printed p. 49); and reduction of body temperature/HR/blood pressure,
removal of metabolic byproducts, endocrine-system recovery, and reduced emotional tension
(cool-down, Table 2.11, PDF p. 69, printed p. 58). **Contested — flag directly:** Issurin's
cool-down rationale explicitly frames blood lactate and "other acid metabolites" as "waste
products" to be "removed" from the muscles (PDF p. 68-69, printed pp. 57-58), citing a
specific clearance kinetic (blood lactate removal after a 4-minute exhausting time trial
takes about 20 minutes, Juel et al., 1990). This is in tension with a modern-physiology
claim already captured in this library's Verkhoshansky staging
([[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--lactate-and-oxygen-debt-myths]], `proven`): lactate is
not a toxin causing soreness or requiring active "removal," and it clears from the blood on
its own within about an hour of strenuous exercise regardless of cool-down activity, with
current research attributing post-exercise soreness to muscle/connective-tissue microtrauma
rather than residual lactate. The specific clearance-time citation (20 minutes for a 4-minute
time trial) may still be a real kinetic fact — that is not itself disputed here — but
Issurin's *framing* of this as evidence that cool-down actively "removes" a harmful waste
product reflects the outdated "lactic acid as toxin" model the Verkhoshansky entry corrects.
Cite this book's clearance-time number without repeating its waste-product framing.

**When to apply** — The Ekstrand et al. (1983) result is directly relevant to Applied
Performance's collaboration with Athletic Medicine on injury reduction: a structured,
medically-supervised warm-up/cool-down protocol is associated with a large, measured
reduction in soft-tissue injury incidence in a team sport, over a real six-month season, not
an acute lab measure. The cool-down-stretching timing finding (Moller et al., 1985) suggests
cool-down, not just warm-up, is where a stretching series may do more for next-day range of
motion.

**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — This is an observational, non-randomized team-level
comparison (teams chose or were assigned to conditions; individual randomization is not
described), and the intervention bundled multiple changes at once (warm-up content, cool-down
content, and medical/physiotherapy supervision), so the four-fold injury reduction cannot be
attributed to warm-up or cool-down alone — Issurin himself flags this study as "atypical
because it refers to the complex effects of warming-up, cooling-down and medical supervision"
(PDF p. 58, printed p. 47). **Contested:** stretching's effect on preventing delayed-onset
muscle soreness specifically is described by Issurin himself as disputed within this same
chapter — "supported by several studies (Hartfield, 1985) and contradicted by others (High
et al., 1989)" (PDF p. 70, printed p. 59) — do not cite stretching-prevents-DOMS as settled.

**Example** — A Baylor position group's practice-ending routine that pairs light locomotion
with a stretching series (rather than stretching only in the pre-practice warm-up) has some
support here for next-day range-of-motion benefit, though the causal strength of the
underlying Moller et al. (1985) study for injury outcomes specifically (as opposed to ROM)
is not established by this citation.

**Related** — [[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--lactate-and-oxygen-debt-myths]] (staging;
the direct source of the lactate-framing contest above — recommend the Verkhoshansky entry
add a reciprocal link back to this one once both are reviewed).

# Which Training Modalities Tolerate Fatigue, and Which Need a Fresh Athlete

**What it is** — Figure 2.3 (PDF p. 72, printed p. 60) ranks eleven training modalities by
how much athlete fatigue they can tolerate before the acute training effect is compromised,
from "well rested" through "slightly fatigued," "moderately fatigued," to "fatigued":
**require well-rested or only slightly fatigued athletes** — maximal speed (least
fatigue-tolerant of all), acquisition of new technical skills, explosive strength, maximal
strength (neural mechanism, e.g. 1-3RM); **tolerate up to moderate fatigue** — anaerobic
glycolytic power, technique perfection, aerobic power, maximal strength (hypertrophy, e.g.
8-10RM); **tolerate fatigue through to the end of the session (most fatigue-tolerant)** —
anaerobic glycolytic capacity/endurance, aerobic endurance (long duration), strength
endurance, flexibility. Issurin's stated reasoning (PDF pp. 71-73, printed pp. 60-62):
exercises needing precise excitatory neural output (max speed, explosive strength, technical
skill acquisition, neural-mechanism strength) are blocked by inhibitory CNS output in
fatigued athletes, so they belong early; anaerobic glycolytic power needs available energy
reserves that are depleted in fatigued athletes; hypertrophy-strength work depends on total
mechanical work and post-exercise recovery conditions (not the athlete's pre-exercise
freshness), so it can be placed later or even after an endurance session; anaerobic
glycolytic capacity and strength/aerobic endurance work are defined by sustained effort
*despite* accumulating fatigue, so some fatigue is expected and even required for the
intended stimulus.

**Why it works** — CNS-dependent, high-precision, high-velocity qualities are limited by
inhibitory neural output and available energy stores that both degrade with fatigue,
while volume/duration-dependent qualities (hypertrophy, strength/aerobic endurance) depend
on total accumulated work or post-session recovery rather than the athlete's moment-to-moment
freshness — so sequencing exists to protect the fatigue-sensitive qualities' window, not
because "harder exercises always go first."

**When to apply** — Ordering exercises within a single practice or lift: place max-speed
work, new skill acquisition, explosive strength, and low-rep neural-strength work at the
start of a session (or after only light warm-up fatigue); place hypertrophy work, technical
perfection under fatigue, and long-duration aerobic/strength-endurance work later, when some
accumulated fatigue is acceptable or even intended. Issurin gives a worked example (PDF
p. 72, printed p. 61): an endurance athlete needing to preserve muscle mass can have a
hypertrophy-focused strength session (8-10RM) placed *after* a medium-load endurance
session, because hypertrophy's driver is total mechanical work and post-workout recovery
conditions, not pre-workout freshness — this would be the wrong sequencing choice for a
neural-strength (1-3RM) session, which does need "prime time."

**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — **The author gives no primary citation for Figure 2.3
itself** — it reads as the author's own synthesized ranking rather than a reproduced,
independently-sourced scale; treat the ordinal ranking (which modality is more or less
fatigue-tolerant than its neighbor) as a reasonable but unvalidated synthesis, not a measured
result. The figure gives no guidance on *how much* fatigue is "slight" vs. "moderate" in
objective terms (RPE, HR, or specific fatigue markers), so applying it requires a coach's own
judgment call about where an athlete currently sits on that continuum. It also does not
address multi-session days directly — see [[heuristic--two-a-day-workout-sequencing-by-dominant-ability]]
for cross-session sequencing.

**Example** — A football practice combining new install (technical skill acquisition) with
conditioning: install work belongs at the start of practice when players are fresh and can
attend to technical detail; conditioning work belongs at the end, where sustained effort
under fatigue is the intended stimulus rather than a limitation.

**Related** — [[framework--key-workout-and-key-exercise-concept]],
[[principle--training-modality-compatibility-in-a-workout]].

# Structuring Two-a-Day (and Denser) Training Days by Dominant Ability and Rest Interval

**What it is** — Issurin describes how high-performance programs structure multiple same-day
sessions, most commonly two-a-days but up to four (routine in training-camp practice) or
occasionally six (an "exception," per anecdotal coach reports, PDF p. 76, printed p. 65). For
a four-session aerobic-development day (Figure 2.5, PDF p. 77, printed p. 66): session 1
(early morning) uses small load — warm-up, alactic bouts combined with medium-intensity
aerobic work, addressing morning stiffness/soreness; session 2 (mid-morning, after a
multi-hour break) uses medium/substantial load — aerobic interval series combined with
technical tasks, where sprint bouts interact positively with the aerobic work; session 3
(early afternoon, after a one-hour break) uses medium/substantial load — concentrated aerobic
work; session 4 (late afternoon, after a three-hour break) uses substantial load — continuous
aerobic exercise and aerobic-resistance work, with an emphasized, longer cool-down given
accumulated fatigue. For anaerobic-development days (Figure 2.6, PDF p. 78, printed p. 67):
session 2 uses substantial load for anaerobic glycolytic power (fast lactate/oxygen-debt
accumulation); the one-hour break before session 3 allows roughly 70-80% of accumulated
lactate to be oxidized (Volkov, 1986), so session 3's anaerobic glycolytic capacity work
still starts with an already-activated glycolytic/enzymatic system; session 4 (after a
three-hour break, athletes arriving fatigued) targets anaerobic strength endurance,
deliberately sustaining progressive fatigue. For the more common two-a-day structure, Table
2.13 (PDF p. 79, printed p. 68) gives compatible first/second-workout pairings by dominant
ability: aerobic power/capacity — fartlek (10-15s sprint, 3-6min at anaerobic threshold)
first, aerobic interval series second; anaerobic glycolytic power/capacity — anaerobic power
interval series first, anaerobic capacity interval series second; maximal speed — anaerobic
alactic interval series first, anaerobic alactic plus explosive strength exercises second;
techno-tactical abilities — techno-tactical simulation/maximum speed first, match/scrimmage
second.

**Why it works** — The break length between sessions determines how much of the prior
session's fatigue and metabolic byproduct load has cleared before the next session begins,
and the daily plan deliberately exploits this: shorter breaks (one hour) leave residual
glycolytic activation that *helps* a subsequent glycolytic-capacity session, while longer
breaks (three hours) still leave athletes fatigued enough that only fatigue-tolerant
modalities (strength endurance, continuous aerobic work) are appropriate for the day's final
session.

**When to apply** — Directly applicable to football fall-camp scheduling, where two-a-day
sessions are standard. **Eric's baseline** names a specific priority stack for fall camp —
"Goal 1, alactic and aerobic capacity/power for fall-camp demands" (`method-baseline.md`,
"Conditioning and energy systems," citing `class-4-2026.md` pp.34, 39) — and Table 2.13's
maximal-speed pairing (anaerobic alactic interval series both sessions, explosive strength
added to the second) is a directly relevant template for structuring a two-a-day built
around that same alactic/aerobic priority.

**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — Issurin gives no controlled-study citation for the
specific figures in this section (session load levels, the four-session structure, the
70-80% lactate-oxidation-in-one-hour figure attributed to Volkov, 1986, is the one sourced
number; the rest of the daily-series structure reads as the author's own applied synthesis).
The four-session model is explicitly noted as less common in practice than the two-a-day.
**Inference:** none of this section's examples are football-specific (they are framed around
individual/endurance-and-power sports generally); the specific break lengths (one hour,
three hours) and load progressions should be treated as a template to adapt, not a
prescription to copy directly into a football fall-camp schedule without accounting for
football-specific factors (equipment, heat, practice structure, position-group differences)
not addressed in this chapter.

**Example** — A fall-camp two-a-day built around the department's stated alactic/aerobic
priority could pair a morning session of alactic interval sprint work with an afternoon
session combining more alactic work and explosive strength (per Table 2.13's maximal-speed
row), rather than defaulting to a generic "conditioning AM, lift PM" split that does not
target a specific dominant ability across the two sessions.

**Related** — [[claim--morning-resistance-training-no-decrement-after-6hr-rest]],
[[heuristic--exercise-sequencing-by-fatigue-state]],
[[principle--training-modality-compatibility-in-a-workout]].

# Lactate Does Not "Poison" Muscle or Cause Soreness; "Oxygen Debt" Is an Outdated Concept

**What it is** — Two corrections to common misconceptions. (1) Muscle fatigue is not due
to "lactic acid poisoning"; lactate formation is accompanied by hydrogen ions that increase
acidity and can interfere with contraction and enzyme efficiency, but lactate itself is not
the toxin popularly described, and blood lactate returns to normal within about an hour of
strenuous interval training — well before delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS) typically
peaks. The most pronounced soreness actually occurs after prolonged endurance efforts kept
below the lactate threshold, so current theory attributes soreness to transient muscle
cell or connective tissue damage, not lactic acid. (2) The classic "oxygen debt" concept
(the idea that post-exercise heavy breathing "repays" an oxygen deficit incurred during
anaerobic work) is now considered outdated; the post-exercise period instead reflects
recovery oxygen consumption used to regenerate ATP and CP and restore respiratory, ionic,
circulatory, hormonal, and thermal systems to baseline (McArdle, Katch & Katch, 1991). The
text says the former "anaerobic threshold" is now referred to as the "blood lactate
threshold (or turnpoint) or OBLA (Onset of Blood Lactate Accumulation)" (printed 78). (PDF
pp. 87, 89, printed pp. 76, 78.)

**Why it works** — Both corrections reflect the same underlying update in exercise
physiology: lactate is a normal metabolic byproduct and fuel source, not an anaerobic waste
product to be "cleared" or "repaid," and glycolysis runs alongside oxidative metabolism
rather than only replacing it when oxygen is absent (also noted in this book: glycolysis
dominates during sprinting even though muscles have adequate oxygen).

**When to apply** — **Inference:** useful for correcting persistent coaching-room and
classroom misconceptions (e.g. in HHPR 5355 teaching) — "lactic acid causes the burn and
next-day soreness" and "you're paying back oxygen debt after a sprint" are both outdated
framings that this entry can directly correct with citable sources.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** correcting the mechanism does not mean lactate is
irrelevant to training; the blood lactate threshold (OBLA) remains a legitimate, useful
marker for endurance training intensity and athlete conditioning status — only the
"lactic acid as toxin/soreness cause" framing and the "oxygen debt" framing are being
corrected here, not the practical value of lactate-threshold-based training zones.
Inference: the H+/acidosis fatigue mechanism the authors give here (increased acidity
"can interfere with the muscle contraction process") is itself contested in modern work
(Westerblad, Allen & Lannergren 2002, News Physiol Sci 17:17; Allen, Lamb & Westerblad
2008, Physiol Rev 88:287); `proven` here covers only the two named corrections (lactate is
not the cause of DOMS; oxygen debt is replaced by recovery oxygen consumption and EPOC),
not the H+/acidosis fatigue mechanism.

**Example** — **Inference:** an athlete sore two days after a hard endurance session is
more likely dealing with muscle/connective tissue microtrauma than residual lactate, which
would have cleared within an hour; recovery guidance should be based on that, not on
"flushing out lactic acid."

**Related** — [[claim--energy-system-contribution-by-sport-table]].

# Concentrated Loading and Planned Overreaching

**What it is** — A short period of deliberately high, "saturated" training load on one quality (planned overreaching), followed by restitution. Performance is *suppressed* during the loading block and rebounds — supercompensates — afterward. Siff and Verkhoshansky note gains may appear **4 to 12 weeks** after the concentrated block ends; the longer/larger the loading, the longer the delay before performance lifts. The **conjugated sequence** extends this: concentrate on one emphasis (e.g. strength) while holding maintenance loads elsewhere, then shift emphasis in the unloading block so a different quality rises.

**Why it works** — Saturating a stimulus drives a deeper adaptive signal than steady loading. Monitoring via the **testosterone:cortisol (T:C) ratio** tracks the anabolic–catabolic balance: ≥3 weeks of concentrated load lowers the basal T:C ratio (a catabolic shift, reduced preparedness); returning load to normal lets the T:C ratio and performance supercompensate. T:C indexes *preparedness*, not overtraining per se.

**When to apply** — Advanced athletes who can tolerate high loads; building a potent stimulus before a taper/peak; reducing long-term work volume versus concurrent training; timing a delayed performance rebound to a competition window.

**When NOT to apply** — Not for novices or athletes without the training capacity to absorb saturating loads — fatigue is substantial during accumulation and mismanagement tips into overtraining. The delayed-rebound timing (4–12 wk) must be planned backward from competition, or the peak lands in the wrong week. Builds on [[principle--supercompensation-cycle]] and [[framework--step-loading-paradigm]]; bounded by [[principle--individualization]].

**Example** — A 3-week strength-concentrated block (strength up, speed maintained) is timed so the performance rebound surfaces ~4–6 weeks later at the first key competition; T:C ratio is monitored to confirm the post-block recovery.

# Concentrated Loading and Planned Overreaching

**What it is** — A short period of deliberately high, "saturated" training load on one quality (planned overreaching), followed by restitution. Performance is *suppressed* during the loading block and rebounds — supercompensates — afterward. Siff and Verkhoshansky note gains may appear **4 to 12 weeks** after the concentrated block ends; the longer/larger the loading, the longer the delay before performance lifts. The **conjugated sequence** extends this: concentrate on one emphasis (e.g. strength) while holding maintenance loads elsewhere, then shift emphasis in the unloading block so a different quality rises.

**Why it works** — Saturating a stimulus drives a deeper adaptive signal than steady loading. Monitoring via the **testosterone:cortisol (T:C) ratio** tracks the anabolic–catabolic balance: ≥3 weeks of concentrated load lowers the basal T:C ratio (a catabolic shift, reduced preparedness); returning load to normal lets the T:C ratio and performance supercompensate. T:C indexes *preparedness*, not overtraining per se.

**When to apply** — Advanced athletes who can tolerate high loads; building a potent stimulus before a taper/peak; reducing long-term work volume versus concurrent training; timing a delayed performance rebound to a competition window.

**When NOT to apply** — Not for novices or athletes without the training capacity to absorb saturating loads — fatigue is substantial during accumulation and mismanagement tips into overtraining. The delayed-rebound timing (4–12 wk) must be planned backward from competition, or the peak lands in the wrong week. Builds on [[principle--supercompensation-cycle]] and [[framework--step-loading-paradigm]]; bounded by [[principle--individualization]].

**Example** — A 3-week strength-concentrated block (strength up, speed maintained) is timed so the performance rebound surfaces ~4–6 weeks later at the first key competition; T:C ratio is monitored to confirm the post-block recovery.

# Issurin 2016 — Benefits and limitations of block-periodized preparation

> **Citation**
> Issurin, V. B. (2016). Benefits and limitations of block periodized training approaches to athletes' preparation: A review. *Sports Medicine, 46*(3), 329–338. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-015-0425-5

## Why it was promoted

This review distinguishes concentrated-unidirectional and multi-targeted block models and provides a useful conceptual vocabulary for discussing concentrated workloads and sequencing.

## Research question

What benefits, limitations, and sport-context boundaries are reported for two versions of block-periodized athlete preparation?

## Population and context

- The review emphasizes elite, subelite, and well-trained athletes across endurance, team, combat, dual, jumping, and strength/power settings. [p. 11]
- It also discusses a smaller number of recreational-athlete studies.
- It is a training-theory review, not evidence specific to collegiate American football.

## Study design and methods

- Narrative review contrasting concentrated-unidirectional and multi-targeted block-periodization models.
- The article summarizes prior studies in tables but does not report a systematic search, eligibility process, formal risk-of-bias appraisal, or meta-analysis.
- Consequently, the stated number and direction of supportive studies should be interpreted as an author-curated synthesis rather than a pooled comparative estimate.

## Key findings

- Concentrated-unidirectional programs in combat and team sports improved some fitness measures, but the reviewed studies did not report effects on team practice or competitive performance. [p. 6]
- In an elite-swimmer example, specific strength and anaerobic capacity improved but swimming performance improved in only two of three athletes. [p. 6]
- The author judged the concentrated-unidirectional evidence insufficient for broad implementation in high-performance combat, team-sport, and swimming preparation. [p. 6]
- The review reports support from 28 studies for multi-targeted block programs, but the designs, populations, outcomes, and comparator quality varied. [p. 11]
- The concentrated-unidirectional model was presented as better suited to sports dominated by a narrow target quality and as restricted when peak performance requires many interacting abilities. [p. 11]

## Limitations and applicability

- Non-systematic study selection and absent risk-of-bias assessment create a substantial risk of selective emphasis.
- Fitness improvements are not interchangeable with sport-specific performance, availability, or competitive outcomes. [p. 6]
- Training models were not consistently isolated from total volume, intensity, exercise choice, coaching, or athlete history.
- Evidence spans dissimilar sports and training levels; it does not supply validated block durations or effect estimates for collegiate American football.
- The strong conclusion favoring multi-targeted block periodization is the author's synthesis and should not be treated as settled comparative evidence. [p. 11]

## Practitioner interpretation

Use block periodization as a planning hypothesis: concentrate compatible emphases when competition structure and athlete needs justify it, while maintaining the qualities and technical exposure that cannot safely decay. Judge the plan by sport-specific performance, availability, and individual response—not by the periodization label. Compare it prospectively with the program's own prior practice where feasible.

## Evidence map

| Claim | Locator | Evidence type |
|---|---|---|
| Review scope and distinction between two models | p. 4 | narrative framing |
| Concentrated-unidirectional evidence and performance gaps | p. 6 | narrative synthesis |
| Multi-targeted evidence claim and applicability boundaries | p. 11 | narrative synthesis/limitation |

## Related knowledge

- [[periodization]] — annual and phase planning
- [[training-load-concentration]] — sequencing compatible emphases

# "Exercise Selection Matters More Than Intensity and Volume"

**What it is** — Moyer's loudest claim in Lesson 8 ("let me say that a little bit louder for the people in the back"), attributed to Bondarchuk's transfer-of-training work. **Exercise selection matters more for transfer than intensity or volume.** From it he draws a practical rule, which he credits to Bondarchuk, Issurin and Natalia Verkhoshansky: **find the exercises that transfer, then build a

**Why it works** — The mechanism offered is transfer specificity. If an exercise shares few elements with the sprint, adding load or volume only adds adaptation that does not carry over. Bondarchuk goes further (quoted): developing "unnecessary muscle groups" has unavoidable negative effects in speed-strength events. Variations of a transferring exercise are said to keep the stimulus new (Zatsio

**When to apply** — As a design prompt, not a law. When a football player's speed has stalled despite rising strength numbers, look at *what* he does before *how much*. Build variation families around exercises that visibly change sprint mechanics: banded knee drive → cycled → with wearable load → explosive front lunge with knee drive.

**When NOT to apply** — This is `untested` for three reasons. (1) The evidence is a retrospective questionnaire study reported second-hand. Moyer does not give its design, and correlation between general-lift gains and competition decline has obvious confounders (training age, specialisation timing, the decline in general work that normally comes with qualification). (2) Bondarchuk's population 

**Example** — A slot receiver's back squat rose 40 lb over winter while his fly-10 stayed flat. Under this claim, the next block keeps the squat at maintenance and puts the new time into a variation family of pawback and knee-drive special exercises. Whether the fly-10 then moves is the test. The claim itself does not guarantee it.

**Related** — [[principle--sprint-transfer-motor-ability-vs-motor-skill]]; [[principle--progressive-overload-threshold]] — tension: Bompa treats load progression as the primary driver of adaptation; Moyer/Bondarchuk rank selection above load for transfer.

Out of scope: `framework--microcycle-types-and-load-wave-design.md` appeared in the folder during the review. It is Chapter 3 work from another batch and was not reviewed.

## Locator convention (read first)

- Entries cite the **0-based PDF index = printed page + 11**. This holds throughout Ch1-2, and I confirmed it on every cited page.

- **Boundary check (end-exclusive extractor):** idx 25 (kayaker study, printed 14) and idx 44 (low/mid-level carve-out and five-benefit list, printed 33) are both used by entries. idx 45-46 and 84-86 are references. Chapter 2's references run to printed 75 / idx 86, not 73 / 84, but nothing substantive is lost. No content at a range boundary is missing.

## Missing (up to 5 ideas in the covered pages with no entry)

1. **Development-workout count over total volume** (PDF 54-55 / pp.43-44). The BPC "postulates absolute priority of the total number of development workouts as the crucial factor". Worked example: a canoeist's 40-45 km/week at near-threshold, concentrated into three or four development workouts not combined with glycolytic tasks, instead of spread across nine mixed sessions ("permanently fatigued ... training effect small to negligible"). Noakes' "alternate hard and easy days" is offered as the analogue. This is the concentration principle's most practical weekly rule.
2. **Gal Friedman key-exercise case** (PDF 65 / p.54, Fig 2.2). A windsurfing gold medalist replaced long sea sessions with 6 × 1.5-min pumping efforts with 1.5-min easy intervals, at HR peaks of 178 against a personal max of 198 (≈90%), monitored by HR (Yanilov-Eden 2005). `_book.md` names it as an `untested` anecdote, but it was never written.
3. **Warm-up structure and dosing** (PDF 59-62 / pp.48-51). General part 8-15 min to HR 110-130, then special part 10-20 min (Table 2.7). Active dynamic before passive stretching. Standard vs non-standard special warm-up (Table 2.8), and "frequent utilization of a particular warm-up ... reduces its stimulatory effect". Also the coach-interview claim that at least half of musculoskeletal injuries are partly or wholly caused by insufficient warm-up (PDF 59 / p.48), which is `untested` and anecdotal.
4. **Six-step workout construction algorithm** (Table 2.14, PDF 81 / p.70), with cool-down dosing: cool-down usually 10-20 min, "not enough after sessions with extreme workloads" (PDF 70 / p.59). Also catecholamines can stay raised 24 h or more after a marathon or triathlon (PDF 69 / p.58).
5. **Why block training emerged: fewer training hours, more competition days** (Figs 1.5-1.6, PDF 27-29 / pp.16-18). 2. **Gal Friedman key-exercise case** (PDF 65 / p.54, Fig 2.2). 3. Residual-effects claim: rewrite the Eric-contradiction paragraph (class-1 agrees with class-4 on ordering; the course cites Issurin), fix the 40-90% scope, fix the Thorstensson citation, fix the Example arithmetic.

**Verdict: GO AFTER FIXES. 0 GO, 17 FIX, 0 NO-GO** (16 entries plus `_book.md`). Every error has an exact correction, and none reverses a rule in the book.

I opened every cited page as an image (printed pp. 1-73). All the numbers I checked match their pages: Tables 1.5, 1.6, 2.3, 2.4 and 2.10, plus the Spreuwenberg, Ekstrand, Woolstenhulme and Moller studies. No entry uses `proven`.

Report: `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV\Flint\.claude\worktrees\step1-triage\staging\review_issurin_ch1-2_opus.md`

**Your four extra checks**
- **Table 1.6:** all five values match the page (PDF 35 / p.24): aerobic endurance 30±5, maximum strength 30±5, anaerobic glycolytic endurance 18±4, strength endurance 15±5, maximum speed 5±3 days. Two text errors sit around the table:
  - The 40-90% increase applies to aerobic enzymes only, not the whole list.
  - The sprint percentages carry no citation on the page. Thorstensson (1988) is cited on the next page (PDF 36 / p.25) for a different point.
- **Eric's contradiction:** it exists, but not as the entry describes it.
  - `class-4-2026.md` p.47 does conflict with Table 1.6 (it says aerobic is lost fastest, alactic slowest).
  - The class-1 transcript agrees with class-4 on that order. It says aerobic is "lost very quickly" (marker pp.25 and 28). Its 30-day figures assume a small retention load. Its 5-day speed figure is about tissue readiness: "the nervous system doesn't change a whole lot".
  - The entry says neither source cites the other. That is false: `week1-lecture.md` marker p.64 cites "Issurin (Block Training Text)", and p.66 reproduces the table, giving strength endurance as ~12 days instead of 15±5.
- **Lactate contest:** unfair to both sides. Rewrite it as a disagreement over terms only.
  - Issurin never calls lactate a toxin or a cause of soreness. He links soreness to eccentric work, and he cites Bonen & Belcastro (1976) for faster clearance with light activity.
  - The Supertraining entry never says lactate clears "regardless of cool-down activity". The two sources agree on clearance time.
- **Case studies:** both are `untested`. The canoe entry states the population. The Bondarchuk entry needs one added clause.

**Fixes that apply to every entry**
- **G1:** invented football examples and "When to apply" applications carry no "Inference:" label.
- **G2:** em dashes in body text. The dashes in section headers are house style and can stay.
- **G3:** "well-documented" and "standard extension" appear without a citation.
- **G4:** the entries say Issurin's 2016 review is not cached, but it is already in the vault (`research-papers/issurin-2016-benefits-and-limitations-...md`). Link it.
- **G5:** "independently arrived at" is false. Eric's course deck cites Issurin and teaches his three block types, his residual-effect table and his compatibility chart.

**Major fixes**
1. **`heuristic--exercise-sequencing-by-fatigue-state`**
   - Problem: Figure 2.3 is at PDF 71 / p.60 and has 12 modalities, not 11. Three are in the wrong group. Anaerobic glycolytic power belongs with slightly fatigued (read from the figure). Anaerobic glycolytic capacity belongs with moderately fatigued (text, PDF 82 / p.71). Technique perfection belongs with fatigued (text, PDF 73 / p.62).
   - Correction: the full regrouping is in the report.
2. **`heuristic--two-a-day-workout-sequencing-by-dominant-ability`**
   - Problem: the book says two- and three-workout days are routine in camp and six is an exception. The entry says four are routine. Its Figure 2.5 contents are shifted one session (PDF 77 / p.66): alactic bouts belong to session 2, not session 1.
   - Correction: use the full session table in the report. Label "two-a-days are standard in football fall camp" as Inference, and check it against current NCAA DI preseason rules and Baylor's camp schedule.
3. **`claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability`**
   - Problem: the contradiction and origin claims are wrong, as described above.
   - Correction: rewrite the contest paragraph. Scope the 40-90% to aerobic enzymes and fix the Thorstensson citation. Fix the Example: 4+3+2 weeks puts competition 35 days after accumulation ends, at the edge of the 30±5 window. Add Issurin's own taper-detraining note (PDF 34 / p.23).
4. **`case-study--warmup-cooldown-injury-reduction-soccer`**
   - Problem: the lactate contest (see above). The cool-down has four objectives, not three. Ekstrand is a controlled trial, not "observational".
   - Correction: rewrite the contest as terms only. Fix the locators: waste framing at PDF 67-69, Juel's 20 minutes at PDF 70 / p.59.

**Other fixes**
5. **`principle--concentration-of-training-workloads`**
   - Problem: `contested` rests on Bompa & Haff, but the vault ingested only their Ch1-2, and that material agrees with Issurin. The related link `framework--block-periodization-mesocycle-taxonomy` is broken. Table 1.4 literally says "sufficient energy supply" (an apparent typo) and the entry silently changes it.
   - Correction: base `contested` on the vault Issurin 2016 brief (its pp.6, 11). Relink to `framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles`. Record the typo.
6. **`framework--training-stage-and-multi-peak-annual-cycle`**
   - Problem: printed p.29 lists four benefits. The five-item list that includes peaking is at PDF 44 / p.33, and Table 1.8 has no benefits list. `contested` has the same Bompa problem.
   - Correction: fix the locators, add the carbohydrate clause, and base `contested` on the 2016 brief.
7. **`framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles`**
   - Problem: Table 1.7 is at PDF 38 / p.27. The Example invents 3-4 / 3-4 / 1-2 week blocks.
   - Correction: use the book's 4/4/2 weeks (PDF 33 / p.22) and its 2-6 week block length. Replace "independently arrived at" with the course's Issurin citation.
8. **`principle--training-modality-compatibility-in-a-workout`**
   - Problem: Figure 2.4 is at PDF 74 / p.63. The technical-learning row is misread: other modalities come after the learning task. The Example demotes new install to a later slot, which breaks Figure 2.3.
   - Correction: fix the locator and the row. Change juniors' "need" to "may be". Note that the class-1 lecture teaches Figure 2.4 itself.
9. **`case-study--concurrent-training-interference-and-decay`**
   - Problem: the swimmer study is called "controlled", but it is an uncited single group with no control. The entry blends the energy and fatigue mechanisms. In the kayaker case, only strength work was called "harmful for racing technique".
   - Correction: remove "controlled", separate the two mechanisms, and fix the attribution.
10. **`claim--multi-peak-annual-preparation-elite-track-and-field`**
    - Problem: the quotes are at PDF 23 / p.12. The 155-day figure is the writer's own sum.
    - Correction: fix the locator and label the 155 days as Inference.
11. **`case-study--bondarchuk-hammer-throw-block-mesocycles`**
    - Problem: the population is missing, and "directly inspired Issurin" is unsupported (the book cites both side by side, PDF 34 / p.23). The book says "1988 and other" Olympics.
    - Correction: add "elite Soviet male hammer throwers, one Olympic final". Drop "directly inspired". Add the exercise-rotation feature (PDF 32 / p.21).
12. **`case-study--issurin-kaverin-canoe-kayak-block-periodization`**
    - Problem: the book says "prevailing opinion", not "the author and colleagues". The 4/4/2 durations are missing.
    - Correction: fix the wording, add the durations, and label "his own national team" as Inference.
13. **`framework--key-workout-and-key-exercise-concept`**
    - Correction: Table 2.10 is at PDF 66 / p.55. Add the 1-2.5 lactate band to the restoration row. Label the monitoring-feasibility and force-plate-metrics analogies as Inference.
14. **`framework--workout-load-classification-and-rpe-mapping`**
    - Problem: the coordination-workout point is misstated. Issurin compares against the restoration-time scale, not against RPE (PDF 53 / p.42).
    - Correction: fix the sentence. Note that Table 2.4 is the author's modification of Borg. Fix the G3 phrases.
15. **`claim--morning-resistance-training-no-decrement-after-6hr-rest`**
    - Problem: Issurin frames the study for "dual and team sports" and never names football (PDF 79 / p.68).
    - Correction: say "dual and team sports", label the football application as Inference, and label the Example.
16. **`case-study--postactivation-potentiation-exercise-order-squat-study`**
    - Correction: "the study authors attribute" the power result, not Issurin (PDF 73 / p.62). Label the Example. Add links to the vault's hanson-2007, hirayama-2014 and seitz-2017 notes.
17. **`_book.md`**
    - Correction: say the page offset is a 0-based index, with viewer pages at printed + 12. Fix the section ranges: 1.3 starts at p.30, 2.3 at p.59, and Ch2 runs to p.75 / PDF 86. Fix the 2016-review claim. Add or drop the Gal Friedman example.

**Page boundaries:** nothing substantive is missing at any page-range boundary. PDF 25 and 44 are both used by entries. The Chapter 2 references end at PDF 86, not 84, but those are references only.

**Five ideas no entry captures:**
- Number of development workouts matters more than volume (canoeist example, PDF 54-55).
- The Gal Friedman key-exercise case (PDF 65).
- Warm-up dosing (PDF 59-62).
- The six-step workout algorithm and cool-down dosing (PDF 81, 70).
- The survey data on more competition days and fewer training hours (PDF 27-29).

A new Chapter 3 file, `framework--microcycle-types-and-load-wave-design.md`, appeared in the folder during the review. It is out of scope and I did not review it.
